News.title: Surrogate mum reveals why she refused to abort ‘precious’ baby with heart defect after biological parents sued her
News.content:
MOTHER'S FIGHT Surrogate mum reveals why she refused to abort ‘precious’ baby with heart defect after biological parents sued her

A SURROGATE mum who refused to abort the baby of the couple who hired her has broken her silence for the first time.

McKenna West, 28, gave birth to the child – who has a rare heart defect – against the wishes of biological parents Nasheen Gilkar and Omar Ahmed.



The baby boy, who West named Gabriel, was born on August 12 and has now been handed over to the biological parents – despite their earlier pleas to terminate the pregnancy.

The legal battles between the trio rage on however – and now West has broken her silence on the ordeal and issued a final, desperate plea.



In a bombshell article for the New York Post, West said hearing the order to terminate her pregnancy was the moment “my worst fears came true”.

She said: “It is unthinkable to me to give birth to a precious, living, breathing baby boy and yet deny him the chance to survive.”

The mum-of-two was convinced that the baby she was carrying “had a real chance at a full life”.

Babies with hypoplastic left heart syndrome (HLHS) need to undergo the Norwood procedure – a complex open-heart surgery shortly after birth – followed by two further surgeries.

“As a cardiac nurse, I knew this little one had a great shot at survival if given the opportunity to receive the necessary treatment”, she said.

Californian couple Gilkar and Ahmed had previously agreed to pay West £45,000 to carry their child, court docs say, but changed their mind after discovering the baby had HLHS.



The syndrome means that the child’s heart is too small and cannot pump blood to the rest of his body. It was discovered at week 20 of the pregnancy.

The contract signed between the trio included a clause which stated that West must get an abortion if there were problems with the fetus – but the nurse could not face giving up the baby.

Furious that West broke the terms of their contract, the couple sued the nurse for at least $100,000.



They also cut off payments for the pregnancy – which West then covered herself.

“All I wanted was for the contracting couple to commit to giving this baby lifesaving treatment. But they refused.

“So, I made my own plans to save him.”

The nurse researched the best states for the Norwood procedure – and then moved with her two kids to Texas.

There, West planned to give birth in a hospital with a 100 per cent survival rate for the complex open heart surgery.



A Texan court order forced the couple to allow the necessary medical treatment. Gilkar and Ahmed continue to fight to have this court order thrown out.

In a further devastating twist, West has not been allowed to hold the baby boy she carried and delivered.

“The only glimpse I got of him was during a very short 60 seconds while his umbilical cord was still connected” she recounted, adding “as soon as the cord was cut, he was taken away.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

West sums up the battle like this: “Two sides are in a dispute, but only one of us is committing to lifesaving care.

“My plea, my only goal, is simple: Let’s commit to giving this baby the full treatment he needs to live.”

News.title: More than 350k teens facing GCSE resits as Labour moves to overhaul English and maths system
News.content:
MORE than 350,000 teens face having to resit English or maths GCSEs next year — as Labour moves to overhaul the system.

The scale of the resit crisis emerged as exam results also showed more older pupils are taking the subjects again, but a smaller proportion are passing.



Some 178,270 16-year-olds in England missed the crucial grade 4 GCSE in maths this summer, while about 180,570 fell short in English, according to analysis of Ofqual data.

Post-16 entries — mostly those who have already failed previous years’ resits — soared by 6.5 per cent in English and 5.8 per cent in maths compared with last year. But the pass rates fell by 1.4 percentage points in English and 1.7 points in maths.



Education Secretary Lucy Powell said not getting grade 4 was creating a “blockage” for teens trying to get jobs, apprenticeships or further study.

More than a million 16 to 24-year-olds are not in employment, education or training (Neets).



She wants new Level 1 qualifications in English and maths to help struggling teens build up to resits.

She said: “There’s got to be a better way to give young people the skills and confidence they need to succeed, not just branding them a failure, and also allowing them to gain other qualifications that show they have a strong foundation in English and maths.”

But former Education Secretary Lord Gove blasted a “culture of low expectations” and insisted schools must “consistently raise the bar”.

He told Times Radio: “It is a moral imperative for this country to demand that we end illiteracy and innumeracy, and it is absolutely vital that the Education Secretary should be leading a crusade to get more children to pass examinations.”



Overall, 22 per cent of GCSE entries bagged top grades of 7 or above, up slightly from last year.

But the standard pass rate slipped to 67.3 per cent — back to pre-Covid levels. Girls’ lead over boys in GCSE grades has narrowed to its smallest level on record. For top grades it fell to a 4.8 percentage point lead from 5.1 last year. Girls’ standard pass lead dropped to 5.8 from 6.2.

Refrom UK will clamp down on “Mickey Mouse” degrees such as Gender Studies from mediocre universities and fund apprenticeships, MP Suella Braverman has said.

News.title: College tutor wins the ‘Superbowl of bricklaying’ after laying 859 bricks in an HOUR to take home title
News.content:
A COLLEGE tutor has been crowned the king of British brickies after laying 859 bricks in just one hour.

Dale Wherton won the illustrious Super Trowel event, known as the “Super Bowl of bricklaying”.



He beat 15 other competitors to take home the title and will now take on other champion brickies in Las Vegas next year.

Dale, 35, said it was a “dream come true” to win Super Trowel 2026 at the Hertfordshire Showground in St Albans on August 1.



He got the competitive bricklaying bug at college in Stoke aged 15 before working in the industry for 20 years.

And he has honed his speed skills since becoming a lecturer six months ago at West Nottinghamshire College.



The dad-to-be, from Derby, said: “We have test walls with training mortar which doesn’t set, so we can put up and take down as many as we like.

“I remember 20 years ago my college tutor showed me this event in Vegas and I thought I’d really love to do that.

“Only one other Englishman has won it before as the Americans have dominated.

“Even the world’s best boxers dream of going to Las Vegas to compete. Now I’m doing it to lay bricks.”



Dale will compete in the Spec Mix Bricklayer 500 competition in January in the US.

He said: “I’ll be going there as an Englishman trying to win.”

News.title: Andy Burnham has insisted he will be ‘relentless’ in stopping small boats but latest booklet looks like a welcome pack
News.content:
Home truths

HARD-working Brits are being asked to believe that Labour is getting tough on illegal migration.

But the latest booklet being handed out to those arriving on small boats makes a mockery of that claim.



It encourages asylum seekers to quit taxpayer-funded accommodation and move in with friends or family who already live here.

They’ll be given help with their travel costs and will still receive £49.18 a week for food and essentials.



So what, exactly, is the deterrent?

Andy Burnham has insisted he will be “relentless” in stopping small boats. But this looks less like a crackdown and more like a welcome pack.



The message on the four-page leaflet is clear: Come to Britain, find a spare room and the taxpayer will help you get there. It is handed out alongside a nine-page guide on why raping or abusing women and children isn’t allowed.

Is the Home Office sure the recipients won’t just disappear and get a job in the black economy?

Labour insists the booklets are aimed at making British law clear to new arrivals and helping the drive to close more migrant hotels.

But yet again taxpayers are expected to shoulder the cost of mass illegal migration while ministers fail to come up with an effective deterrent to stop them arriving in the first place.



The PM has said he is “changing the whole approach” to dealing with the Channel crisis. He’s certainly done that.

It looks like he has simply given up.

Revise ideas

THOUSANDS of pupils were celebrating their GCSE results on Thursday — but many will have to go through it all again.

More than 350,000 youngsters face having to resit English or maths next year after failing to reach a crucial grade four.

It is vital that everyone hits the mark in these two important subjects if we are to stop today’s schoolkids joining the jobs scrapheap.



Education Secretary Lucy Powell must tackle low expectations in the classroom as a matter of urgency.

This will requires a fundamental reform of maths and English teaching at secondary schools to support those who struggle to attain a reasonable grasp of the 3Rs.

Failure is not an option.

Battle of bottles

PUBS are already fighting for survival — now Labour is to pile on another hefty bill.

Despite paying for their own recycling, they could be charged again for getting rid of bottles because they are classed as household waste.



Publicans warn it will cost £50million a year — enough to fund 4,400 bar staff or buy 11million pints.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

When pubs are closing their doors, the last thing they need is another tax-like burden.

Give ’em a break!

News.title: Home Office ‘don’t rape’ leaflet proves leftie loons know danger of open borders – there’s a simple solution to stop it
News.content:
WELCOME to Britain! Please wipe your feet.

Here in Blighty, our borders are now open to anyone who wants to come here — but we do expect everyone to obey our rules and customs.



If you come to our shores, you will need to learn to queue quietly, say “sorry” when someone else bumps into you, moan ­incessantly about the weather and, if it’s not too much bother, would it be okay if you didn’t rape any women or children, or beat your wives?

While the rest of us might take it for granted that rape, paedophilia and ­domestic abuse are most definitely not an acceptable part and parcel of everyday life in the UK, apparently not everyone does.



Which is why the Home Office has just published a nine-page booklet telling ­illegal migrants arriving in Britain not to commit those crimes.

The document, entitled “Understanding behaviours and expectations in the UK: A guide for asylum seekers”, sets out exactly what those expectations are and is to be handed out to the thousands of Channel migrants, helpfully informing them that rape is a serious crime, as is sex with children under 16.



Sexual harassment in the street is also not allowed, and neither is beating your wife or stopping her from getting a job or studying or, indeed, ­leaving the house when she wants.

What’s so surprising is that the Home Office thought this was necessary.

After all, Government ministers have been at pains to tell us these boat arrivals are desperate asylum seekers fleeing persecution — many of them women and children — not potential ­predators.

And people who have ­protested against these migrants being housed in hotels, bedsits or ex-Army ­barracks in their local areas have been branded racist bigots for ­claiming their new neighbours might be making their streets unsafe.



The Home Office booklet is basically a confession by the Government that they KNOW that some Channel migrants are a clear and present danger to women and children in our country.

Yet they continue to welcome them in their thousands to our shores, with a Channel taxi service, free accommodation and food, and legal aid to fight for the right to stay here.

For the ranks of liberal leftie lanyard loons at the Home Office, sitting on ­Commons benches, in the courts and working in migrant NGOs and charities, the rising tide of rapes, sexual assaults and sexual harassment on our streets is just a small price to pay for the pleasure of living in a NICE country that opens its doors to the world’s desperate hordes.



They simply refuse to face up to the reality that not all cultures are equal and that the whole world doesn’t sign up to Western values of equality and freedom.

Indeed, most of the world doesn’t — and particularly not in countries like ­Afghanistan, Eritrea, Iran, Iraq, Sudan and Somalia, where most asylum seekers are now arriving from.

Time after time, illegal migrants have been charged and convicted of raping and sexually assaulting women and girls, yet often the defence given in court is that they did not know what they were doing was a crime.

In one high-profile case, ­Ethiopian migrant Hadush Kebatu, 41, sexually assaulted a 14-year-old schoolgirl while he was living at the Bell asylum hotel in Epping, telling her that it is normal to marry children “in his country”.

And only this week, two Afghan migrant men, aged in their twenties, appeared in court accused of raping a 14-year-old girl on a London-bound train in February.



If only this booklet had been published before their alleged crime, eh?

How many more lives have to be ­sacrificed on the altar of the woke dogma that insists — against all the evidence — that it is a good idea to allow thousands of young men from medieval cultures into our country to roam our streets freely?

Even now, the Home Office is spending taxpayers’ money fighting a legal bid to force them to publish crime statistics by nationality, so they can continue to try to hide the true scale of the problem.

How many more British women and girls are expendable? How many rapes and sexual assaults will be enough to ­convince the Government that this is too high a price to pay? Because for most of us, ONE is too many.

Booklets and advice are not going to make our streets safer. Neither will ­sharing out the potential rapists “fairly” across the whole country, as the Home Office plans to do. (Out of interest, what do you reckon a “fair share” of ­foreign rapists in your local area would be?)



The solution is simple. Every single ­illegal arrival must be locked in a secure detention camp on Day One.

Their asylum applications must be assessed quickly, and those who fail to provide clear evidence for their claim must be immediately deported back home or anywhere else that will have them — Rwanda, Albania or a rocky outcrop in the middle of the ­Atlantic for all I care.

If the Home Office is so convinced that a booklet telling migrants not to rape will change how they behave, then let’s start handing out booklets on the beaches of Calais telling them it’s a crime to travel by dinghy to Britain. I’m sure it will work.

WHEN HARRY MET REALITY . . .

TALKING of the need for tougher border controls, two more economic migrants will be arriving on our shores soon.



Prince Harry and Meghan shocked the nation with their Megxit announcement in 2020 yet, just six years later, it seems their American dream is over and now we are getting the Great ReMeghration of the Sussexes to Blighty, with their tails between their legs.

It turns out life as Californian celebs isn’t quite as fun – or as lucrative – as they’d hoped. After selling every last ounce of their private lives to Netflix and Spotify and after telling the world every secret in their Oprah Winfrey interview and Harry’s memoir, Spare, there isn’t anything left to hawk.

And, frankly, sales of Meghan’s As Ever brand jam just aren’t going to pay the bills. It also turns out their only cachet was their royal link. Without it, they’ve quickly tumbled down from must-have A-listers to late-night TV show laughing stocks.

Maybe Harry wants to make amends with his family.

Maybe he’s bored. Perhaps he has finally sorted out his security concerns, or the couple think British schools will be better for their young children.



Or possibly they are leaving the US before Harry’s visa is cancelled over his drug-taking confessions. Who knows?

But I suspect what this is REALLY about is Meghan’s desire to see her children, Archie and Lilibet, with their HRH Prince and Princess titles, finally taking their rightful places on that Buckingham Palace balcony alongside the King and Queen, and William and Kate.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

It’s time for Meghan’s next reinvention as we tune in to see the Sussexes’ royal soap opera enter its latest season: The Non-Working Royals Return.

News.title: Flash floods and thunderstorms wreak havoc across Britain as water firms warn of hosepipe restrictions until Christmas
News.content:
BRITAIN was drenched by downpours as flash floods and thunderstorms wreaked havoc.

But water bosses warned the long-awaited deluge would do nothing to ease the worst drought for 50 years.



Thames Water said its hosepipe ban would likely last until at least the end of the year.

The nation’s largest water company serves more than ten million customers across London and the Thames Valley.



It said back-to-back heatwaves and barely a drop of rain for weeks had sparked an unprecedented surge in demand.

Its customers used around 100 million litres more water than normal each day during last month’s scorcher.

Boss Nevil Muncaster said the firm would have to extend current restrictions in order to “protect the environment”.

Other water firms are expected to make similar announcements in the coming days and weeks.

Mr Muncaster said: “The Environment Agency forecast is that it will be drier than normal for the next few months, but we’ll wait and see.

“At the same time, we’re going to make sure we protect the environment, make sure we see our ground flow and river flow restored.



“I think realistically it’s going to be towards the end of the year before that comes off.”

Thames Water is currently among 11 firms that have imposed hosepipe bans restricting more than 27million customers nationwide.

Yesterday’s rainfall was a welcome relief after the driest July since records began 190 years ago.



Vast swathes of the nation have been parched by the hot weather.

But racegoers at York’s Ebor Festival took shelter under brollies.

Cricket fans also took cover as the weather held up play on Day Two of the First Test against Pakistan at Headingley in Leeds.

Meanwhile, motorists on the M6 in Cumbria endured driving rain.

And shoppers and tourists at London’s Trafalgar Square hurried through showers.



Morecambe, Lancs, had more than two inches of rain in 24 hours.

The Met Office said it would be dry for most this weekend before a return to showers next week.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The downpours arrived with three-quarters of England officially in drought.

Some places have gone without a drop for two months and July was southern England’s driest month on record.

News.title: Tragedy as girl, 5, dies after being ‘left in hot car outside home when family forgot she was there after school’
News.content:
HEAT HORROR Tragedy as girl, 5, dies after being ‘left in hot car outside home when family forgot she was there after school’

A YOUNG girl has been found dead after her family allegedly forgot about her and left the child in a boiling hot car.

Family members reported the five-year-old as missing before finding her unresponsive inside a car in Garland, Texas, police say.



Emergency services raced to the scene on Redbird Drive at around 8:20pm on Tuesday to find the youngster in a state of medical emergency.

Cops said the girl and her sibling had been picked up from school by an adult family member – her sibling got out, but the five-year-old did not.



The girl had just started school confirmed the local school district.

Family began searching for her – and then tragically found her still inside the car. Police say she could have been inside for hours.



CPR was performed and she was rushed to a local hospital – but tragically could not be saved.

Police have now launched an investigation into the child’s death.

“There are no words to describe how devastating this can be”, said Officer Matt Pesta, from the Garland Police Department.

He explained: “They started looking everywhere, right? Like you would a child, and then they started looking outside. Is she out there playing? You know, where’s she at? And then somebody located her still in the vehicle.”



No charges have yet been filed.

Counselling support has been offered to the family, police added.

Garland, Texas is currently under an extreme heat weather warning.



So far this year 23 children have died across the US in hot cars, according to data from the National Safety Council.

Last year a reported 34 children died in hot cars, including eight in Texas.

“The death is another wake up call for parents” Amber Rollins Executive Director of charity Kids and Car Safety told CBS.

“One of the biggest contributing factors to children being unknowingly left in vehicles is a shift in that normal daily routine. It doesn’t have to be anything huge.”

Chloe Burke, from the same charity, told KBTX: “Most of these cases are a mix of stress or fatigue, and then a change in routine. This is not a lapse of love. It’s just a lapse of memory, and you know, this could really happen to anyone.”

News.title: Afghan migrants ‘raped and assaulted girl, 14, on train after forcing her onto service’ bound for London
News.content:
TRAIN HORROR Afghan migrants ‘raped and assaulted girl, 14, on train after forcing her onto service’ bound for London

TWO Afghan migrants allegedly raped and assaulted a 14-year-old girl on a train after forcing her onto the London-bound service, a court heard.

Baryalai Rahimi, 25, and Mirebadurahman Sadat, 29, are claimed to have carried out the attack on a South Western Railway service from Sturry to London Bridge in February.

The pair appeared at Inner London Crown Court yesterday, Rahimi in a green shirt and Sadat in a grey jumper.

They were aided in court by Dari and Farsi interpreters, and spoke only to confirm their names.





Rahimi, of Southall in west London, is charged with three counts of rape, two counts of sexual assault, and assault by penetration.

Sadat, of Cricklewood in north west London, is charged with two counts of assault by penetration and two counts of causing or inciting a child to engage in sexual activity.

The pair have both denied all ten charges against them in court.

Following a brief hearing regarding the management of the case, Judge Michael Evans KC remanded Rahimi and Sadat in custody until November 4.

The pair will next appear at court on August 27 for further case management.

News.title: Will Harry's return heal rift with his brother? Don't hold your breath
News.content:
This isn't a regular sibling fallout. It is a deep-rooted fracture filled with anger, resentment and a total loss of trust.

And much of it has played out in public.

The Prince of Wales remains in no mood to forgive and forget. The hurt he feels lingers.

"William is very stubborn," a family friend told the BBC. "To feel cheated by your own brother has been painful. He can't just put it behind him."

But in his interview with the BBC last year, Harry offered a different view.

"I would love reconciliation with my family. There's no point in continuing to fight any more."

The problem for Prince William now is proximity. Harry will be in the UK within two weeks, probably a short drive away from Windsor where William's family lives.

There will be pressure on the elder brother to take the lead, ease the pain and just make up with Harry now the siblings will be living in the same country.

"I think William doesn't care about the pressure to reconcile," said royal author, Valentine Low. "If he doesn't want to reconcile with his brother because of the things he's done, the wrongs that he feels Harry's done to him, he's not going to reconcile. But it does improve the chances I think."

The Prince of Wales will prioritise his public work in the coming months and try not get drawn into the drama around the UK return of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex.

Several people from organisations who have worked with Prince William told BBC News of their desire to support William and help avoid Harry and Meghan becoming a distraction.

One source, who has worked on charity projects with the Royal Family, described wanting to protect the future King.

"This is a hard situation for him full of emotion and anger and we will support him," the source said. "It is really important for me to ensure that any work we do with William will be focused on making a positive change and won't be affected by the Harry and Meghan drama."

News.title: Meghan could return to acting once back in UK
News.content:
The Duchess of Sussex could make a return to acting after she moves back to the UK, according to reports.

Sources close to the Sussexes have not denied reports that Meghan has been offered an acting role in the country.

Australian outlet news.com.au, external first reported that one of the reasons behind Harry and Meghan's decision to return to Britain was that the duchess had been offered a job in an upcoming project.

No details of any role or project have been confirmed. The Sussexes are expected to arrive back in Britain before the end of August, with their children enrolled to start school in September.

As an actress, Meghan was best known for her part in the US legal drama, Suits, in which she played lawyer, Rachel Zane, for seven seasons. Her last episode of Suits aired in 2018.

The duchess put her acting career on hold after her marriage to Prince Harry. At the time, she told the BBC that she did not view quitting acting as giving anything up, but rather as "a new chapter".

She recently returned to acting for the first time in nearly a decade, with a cameo as herself in the upcoming comedy Close Personal Friends, which stars Lily Collins and Brie Larson.

A return to acting could be lucrative for Meghan. The BBC understands that while based in the UK she also hopes to expand the global reach of her US-based lifestyle and cooking brand, As Ever.

News.title: French becoming more effective in stopping small boat crossings, UK says
News.content:
French police tactics are becoming more effective in stopping small boats in the English Channel from reaching Britain, the Home Office has said.

It credits French authorities with intercepting 185 potential crossings involving 4,300 migrants this summer over four separate weeks, as well as stopping 12 boats at sea using new techniques.

Footage released by French police shows officers racing across a beach in jeeps to intercept a launch. Once the boat is abandoned, an officer slashes it lengthways with a knife.

The Conservatives described the announcement as a "joke" and said Channel crossing preventions were "down by half over the past year".

Migrants can be seen throwing objects at the officers, one of whom appears to respond with pepper spray.

While Channel crossings are down about 40% compared to last year, thousands of illegal migrants are getting through with 250 arriving on Monday.

In late July a record 165 migrants reached the UK in a single boat with Border Security Command pictured towing a mega dinghy - estimated to be the same size as a standard bus at 13m (42ft) long - when it arrived in Dover on 23 July.

The Home Office, citing French police figures, said that since it struck a deal with France three months ago which included additional funding for authorities, 61% of small boats have been intercepted - a five per cent increase compared to last year.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said the "UK-France deal is already having a real impact".

The UK-France Border Security deal agreed in April under the Starmer government, includes Â£501m over three years to strengthen operations in northern France and Â£161m for new approaches.

Previously the French authorities allowed most dinghies to head towards the UK once they had launched, because of the risk of intercepting them in deep water, while loaded with people.

Of the 12 dinghies stopped so far at sea, three interceptions took place in the last two weeks.

The techniques being used have not been disclosed by the UK or France.

Charlie Eastaugh, director of maritime and small boats at the Border Security Command, told the BBC that "last Thursday alone, the French prevented all three of the boats that tried to cross".

Speaking to the BBC at the Western Jetfoil facility in Dover used to process migrants, he said: "Two of those they prevented at sea, and one they prevented on land."

News.title: My student day out in London turned to terror - now survivors like me won't be forgotten
News.content:
Travis Frain was texting his mates a photo he had just taken of Big Ben on a university trip to London when his day turned from normal to anything but.

"One of the guys in my group shouted 'look out' and as I looked up from my phone the terrorist's car was in front of me.

"It was a split second really before the car hit me. I went over the bonnet, into the air, before landing back on the ground."

This was 22 March 2017, when attacker Khalid Masood drove his car into crowds, killing four, before stabbing a police officer to death outside Parliament.

Frain, then 19, was left with multiple injuries including a fractured leg, which took two years to heal. "There will always be a part of you affected by that attack."

Now 28, he spoke to BBC News as the UK's first national day for victims and survivors of terrorism is set to take place on Friday.

News.title: The town whose council wants migrants to move in
News.content:
A new shop opened along Greenock's fading High Street in May. Anik African Store has brought a small corner of Nigeria to the Scottish town, selling yams, plantain, okra and catfish.

It is not the only African food shop here - there is another just metres away, responding to the area's changing population.

Five years ago, locals say, it would have been rare to see a black person in Greenock. Now hundreds of Africans and refugees have moved to the area.

The local council has in fact come up with a plan to attract even more to this corner of the west of Scotland as a means of stemming its falling population.

Scottish people "are lovely and accommodating", says Anik's owner, Christianah Omilana, who came to the UK in 2021. "Immigrants will come when there is work", she adds.

News.title: British rapper Yung Filly to face retrial on rape charges in Australia
News.content:
British rapper Yung Filly will face a retrial on three rape charges in Australia, after a jury cleared him of several sexual assault offences but could not reach a decision on others.

The YouTuber, whose real name is Andres Felipe Valencia Barrientos, was charged with repeatedly raping and assaulting a fan after performing at a nightclub in Perth in 2024.

He denied all 10 charges, and last month a jury found him not guilty on three counts of sexual penetration without consent.

He was also acquitted of one assault charge and another of strangulation, but was found guilty of two counts of assault occasioning bodily harm, for which he'll be sentenced after his retrial.

The West Australian court heard that the 31-year-old social media star had consensual sex with a 20-year-old fan in his hotel room, before she alleged he turned violent and ignored her cries to stop.

Barrientos will next appear in court 27 August for an application to vary his bail. A retrial date has not been set.

News.title: Millennials are struggling to buy a home - but is it actually getting easier?
News.content:
Leaving education, getting a job, buying a home and perhaps starting a family: the path previous generations followed may seem a distant dream to many now.

But is it getting a bit easier - at least when it comes to getting on the housing ladder?

Today's prospective first-time buyers may well feel hard done by; they are still worse off than recent generations.

If you were born in the UK in the mid-1990s you've about a 25% chance of owning your own home, as this chart shows.

News.title: Rain to stop in time for weekend as sun returns
News.content:
High pressure is set to build across the UK over the next few days bringing drier weather for the weekend.

Heavy downpours have brought rain to parts in need this week - albeit with some flash flooding - but these are set to ease.

Many areas will see sunny spells across Saturday and Sunday with daytime temperatures climbing again, perhaps to above the August average in parts of the south of England.

However the nights will turn rather chilly.

News.title: Stifling heat and broken toilets: TUI River Cruise passengers tell of their holiday hell
News.content:
Dozens of people have accused TUI River Cruises of operating vessels with faulty facilities including persistently broken air conditioning, after they spent thousands of pounds on holidays.

Earlier this year passengers on the Skyla, a ship operated by TUI, contacted BBC Your Voice to say they had been stranded in Budapest during a heatwave with little to no air conditioning.

Following that report more people got in touch to say they faced similar problems on both the Skyla and its sister vessel, the Isla. They criticised TUI's customer service and said the refunds offered were inadequate.

TUI apologised to customers where trips "fell short of the standards we aim to deliver".

A spokesperson for TUI, said: "We understand the disappointment and frustration caused to affected customers."

Passengers described stifling conditions as well as problems with plumbing after paying thousands of pounds for European cruises, including on the Danube River.

Andy Peach and his wife booked a seven-day trip on the Skyla in June, travelling through Budapest, Vienna and Linz.

It turned out to be "the worst TUI holiday we've ever been on", he said.

Instead of air conditioning, Peach said there were "big blowers" on board, expelling hot air.

"One was in the middle of the corridor, blocking the exit," he said. "It didn't seem to cool the place down."

Temperatures onboard climbed as the holiday went on leaving him "exhausted", he said. By the end of the week, Peach said the air conditioning in cabins had broken too.

On the second-to-last day passengers were transferred to hotels, which Peach said were "really basic".

He and his wife had paid nearly Â£4,000 for the holiday but they were offered only Â£300 as a refund and given 72-hours to accept it.

He said: "TUI know there's problems on these boats, but continue to sell them to people as a full luxury cruise."

News.title: 'Relentless' GCSE resit cycle 'simply not working', school and college leaders say
News.content:
The "relentless" cycle of pupils in England failing and then resitting their GCSEs in maths and English is "simply not working", a leading education union has said.

The Association of School and College Leaders (ASCL) said a "significant proportion" of students fall short of passing those subjects, and that most who retake those exams "face the miserable experience of falling short once again".

Thursday's results data showed nearly one in four maths and English GCSEs in England were taken by students aged 17 and older, mostly young people resitting exams they had previously failed.

The government said it wanted to stop the "endless treadmill of unnecessary resits".

It said it would introduce a new "stepping stone" qualification from 2028 at Level 1 - one level below GCSEs - for students who do not achieve a pass in GCSE maths or English.

Currently, many courses and jobs remain dependent on students securing GCSE passes in those subjects.

But those that miss the grade can find themselves in a continuing loop of resits as they try and try again to pass.

Pepe Di'Iasio, general secretary of ASCL, said the fail-resit cycle was like "force feeding" students a "relentless diet of GCSE English and maths".

"This limits their education and career options and is very likely to be a factor in the large number of young people who end up not in employment, education or training," he said.

Pass rates for students aged 17 and older in English and maths are much lower than 16-year-old students taking the exams for the first time, bringing down overall GCSE grades for all ages across England, Wales and Northern Ireland as a result.

News.title: Academic who accused Jason Arday of plagiarism suspended by university
News.content:
An academic who accused the late Cambridge professor Jason Arday of plagiarism has been suspended from his post at a Belgian university.

Nathan Cofnas, a self-defined "race realist", was among those to question Arday's work and achievements - prompting a weeks-long plagiarism row prior to his death on 14 August.

Cofnas said he was under investigation by Ghent University "for discriminating against Arday".

The university said a staff member had been notified of a "preliminary disciplinary investigation" and suspended as a precaution.

In a statement regarding Arday's death, its rector Petra De Sutter and vice-rector Herwig Reynaert said they took "recent public statements made by a postdoctoral researcher at Ghent University regarding this matter very seriously", and had taken "appropriate action".

They said the university stood for "respect for human dignity and opposes discrimination, hatred and racism".

"We attach great importance to academic freedom and to open academic debate, even when views are controversial. However, that freedom is not unlimited.

"It goes hand in hand with responsibility and may be restricted in order to protect the rights of others."

They said Arday's death should "prompt reflection" and that lessons should be learned "regarding the way we treat one another both within and outside the academic world, particularly when people become the subject of public controversy".

Cofnas works as a postdoctoral researcher at the university's department of philosophy and moral sciences, according to his website.

His role at a Cambridge college was terminated in 2024 after backlash to his view that, under a true meritocracy, black people would "disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment".

News.title: Man charged over Manchester synagogue attack
News.content:
A man has been charged in connection with the Manchester synagogue attack in which two men were killed.

Counter terrorism police said Hekmat Omar Ali Hakim, 49, of St James Road, Higher Broughton, Salford, had been charged with failing to disclose information regarding terrorist activity.

Hakim has been remanded into custody to appear before Westminster Magistrates' Court on Friday.

There have so far been eight arrests in connection with the attack, however this is the first charge that "relates directly" to the morning of 2 October, when two men died as the Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation synagogue was attacked by Jihad Al-Shamie. He was shot by police and died at the scene.

Worshippers Melvin Cravitz, 66, and Adrian Daulby, 53, were killed.

Assistant Chief Constable Rob Potts, from Counter Terrorism Policing North West (CTPNW) , said: "This is a significant development in our investigation, and my thoughts are with all those affected by the attack, particularly the bereaved loved ones and survivors.

"We have updated them and continue to offer them as much support as possible.

"Since the attack took place, we have been unwavering in our commitment to establishing the full picture behind the incident and identifying anybody who may have been involved in any way."

In July, Mohammad Bashir, 31, who planned an attack on a military base with the Manchester synagogue attacker was jailed for life with a minimum term of 17 years.

He drove his friend Jihad Al-Shamie on a 10-hour round trip to conduct hostile reconnaissance at the UK's Defence Academy in Shrivenham, Oxfordshire, on 14 August 2025.

Weeks after that journey, Al-Shamie, 35, was shot dead by police after carrying out the Heaton Park Synagogue attack.

News.title: People smuggler exposed by BBC investigation arrested and charged
News.content:
A convicted people smuggler who was found by the BBC to be living in Leicestershire has been arrested and charged with immigration offences.

Twana Jamal Khdir, an Iraqi national who was once described as "the godfather" of the French migrant camps, previously served a sentence for people smuggling in France.

Last month, the BBC revealed he was now living in the UK.

The BBC has been told he was arrested on Tuesday near Uppingham in a joint operation led by the Midlands Criminal Financial Investigations team, with the support of Leicestershire Police.

He was charged by the Crown Prosecution Service and appeared at Leicester Magistrates' Court on Wednesday.

He pleaded guilty to entering the UK without valid entry clearance, but not guilty to seeking to obtain leave to enter or remain by deceptive means.

He has been remanded in custody and will next appear at Leicester Crown Court on 5 October.

Khdir was given a five-year jail sentence in France in 2016, where authorities described him as one of the most successful people smugglers ever caught.

Prosecutors said the Iraqi Kurd, aged 36 at the time, had earned up to Â£100,000 a week for moving illegal immigrants across the Channel.

News.title: Thunderstorm warnings expire but rain continues to bring risk of floods for UK
News.content:
Heavy showers and thunderstorms will continue to affect large swathes of the UK on Thursday afternoon, bringing the threat of flooding and travel disruption.

A Met Office yellow thunderstorm covering parts of northern England and north Wales expired at 13:00 BST, with focus of heavy downpours shifting southwards across England and Wales.

Drivers are still being warned that wet weather could lead to slippery conditions and flooded roads.

The Environment Agency has issued one flood warning, external for Walverdon Water in Nelson, Lancashire.

Temperatures are also dropping with some places expected to remain below the August average over the next few days.

News.title: BBC DJ Trevor Nelson reveals brain tumour surgery 'went well'
News.content:
BBC DJ and presenter Trevor Nelson has revealed he stepped away from work after being diagnosed with a brain tumour.

Nelson was last on air in June and had announced he was "taking a little break from my work commitments" due to "health issues".

Speaking to his Instagram followers, external, the 62-year-old said that his "world was turned upside down" when a brain tumour was discovered.

He said that he had undergone a "very serious surgery" which "went incredibly well".

Speaking on Instagram on Thursday, Nelson explained: "There's been a lot of speculation as to what's wrong with me, I know that much. My phone's blown up 20 times over with people asking what's wrong with me.

"I felt that I should at least tell you what was wrong with me. I'm not going to go into it all now and I will deep dive into it at a later date so you can hear the full story."

He continued: "I'll tell you this, I was minding my own business and then it was discovered I had a brain tumour.

"I was shocked, my world was turned upside down, it was a shock to myself and close family and friends and you can imagine quite literally my head was all over the place."

News.title: Vapes could lead to health harms in children, doctors warn
News.content:
Vaping could lead to health harms in children and young people and should be made "less attractive" to them, doctors have said.

The Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health (RCPCH) has reviewed about 81 studies into vaping and said it is linked to higher rates of breathing problems and evidence of harm in babies whose mothers used vapes while pregnant.

The review said vaping should not be seen as a "harmless part of growing up".

The RCPCH is calling on the UK government to go further in its proposals to place new restrictions around the sale of vapes and suggests limiting the number of flavours that are available.

The review into vapes has been published in the journal Archives of Disease in Childhood. Experts from the college looked at the studies involving health or social outcomes of vaping on children and young people.

It said vaping had an association with problems including wheezing and coughing, poor oral and dental health, poor sleep, mental health problems and eye symptoms.

Co-author of the systematic review, Prof Will Carroll, said the evidence showed "clear links" with respiratory symptoms, nicotine dependence and subsequent cigarette smoking.

"We must act to make vaping less attractive and accessible to children," he said.

Vice-president for policy of the RCPCH, Dr Mike McKean, added: "Vaping is still a relatively new product, and there is much we do not yet know about its long-term impact on children and young people but a clear and concerning picture is emerging."

"We need to keep pace with a rapidly evolving market and continue to take action to protect children from nicotine products."

In July, the government launched a 12-week consultation on the appearance, packaging and display of vapes with the aim of reducing the appeal of the products to children.

As part of the new proposals, packs would need to be plain with strict limits on branding and only simple flavour descriptions like "apple" or "cola" used.

Other restrictions would move vapes out of sight in shops, similar to how cigarettes and tobacco are currently sold.

The 100-day consultation follows the recent passing of the Tobacco and Vapes Act,, external which sets out proposals to create the UK's first smoke-free generation.

Children aged 17 or younger now face a lifelong ban on buying cigarettes, since it will be illegal for shops to sell tobacco to anyone born after 1 January 2009.

Dr McKean said the new act was "an important step towards protecting children from nicotine addiction, but it must not be seen as a one-and-done solution".

Prof Carroll said the government needed "to go further and limit the types of flavours available to them as opposed to just their descriptions".

There’s something about a gel manicure that just makes you feel like you’ve got it together. The shiny finish, the knowledge that they’re not going to immediately chip during basic everyday tasks (unless you’re really unlucky)... Your life might be falling apart. But your nails? Impeccable.

But the reality might not be quite as glossy. Over the past few years, a spate of headlines and studies have called out various gel nail ingredients as potential red flags for our health. Most recently, those headlines have centred around one specific ingredient, TPO, which is being phased out in the UK. So how worried do we need to be about our favourite beauty habit?

Trimethylbenzoyl diphenylphosphine oxide, mercifully shortened to TPO, is a photoinitiator, a chemical compound that absorbs the light emitted by a UV or LED nail lamp to kickstart the reaction involved in the photocuring process. This hardens the polish and gives the glossy, durable finish that sets gels apart from a traditional manicure (conventional nail varnish doesn’t include TPO, because there is no curing reaction involved in the process – you simply wait for the polish to dry).

It’s been particularly popular in gel polishes because it absorbs light across a wide range of wavelengths, so it works well with various nail dryers. So what’s the issue here? Research on animals has shown that high levels of exposure to TPO could be dangerous to fertility and embryonic development. In 2020, one study found that male rats underwent “massive” changes to their testicles, as well as reduced fertility, while females experienced disruption to their reproductive cycle; another lab study found it to be toxic to human cells.

open image in gallery Gel nails have a glossy, long-lasting finish that sets them apart from traditional manicures ( Getty/iStock )

TPO has since been categorised as a category 1B reproductive toxicant under European Union and UK regulations. It’s important to note that this is very much a precautionary measure. In these studies, the animals and the human cells were exposed to much, much higher dosages of TPO than you would be while getting your nails done; the research on rats, for example, relied on large, repeated doses ingested over an extended period of time. Plus, the photocuring process means that the actual amount of time you’re exposed to TPO is relatively brief; it is consumed by the chemical reaction.

Still, acting out of caution, the European Union banned TPO in September last year, and the UK has now caught up. As of 15 August, manufacturers can’t launch any new products onto the market that feature TPO as an ingredient. Pre-existing products, though, will still be available for salons to purchase and use until 14 February next year, when they won’t be able to buy more stock.

What does this mean for your manicure, then? In truth, it won’t change things much. “There are already TPO-free gel formulations available, which use alternative photoinitiators such as TPO-L to cure the gel under UV or LED light,” explains Dr Derrick Phillips, a consultant dermatologist. Indeed, many salons are already using them – and the wide availability of alternative products was a factor in the ban.

There are already TPO-free gel formulations available, which use alternative photoinitiators such as TPO-L to cure the gel under UV or LED light Dr Derek Phillips, consultant dermatologist

There should, Phillips adds, “be little noticeable difference in the finish, durability or overall quality of a well-formulated TPO-free manicure” – and you might already be going TPO-free without even realising it. And if you’re worried, you can just ask your nail technician about the ingredients.

But concerns around gel manicures go beyond TPO. That’s because the photoinitiating process also involves a UV or LED light that emits low levels of UVA radiation, which is linked to a higher risk of cancer.

A study published in Nature Communications in 2023 exposed mouse cells and human cells to UV nail dryers for 20 minutes, and found that between 20 and 30 per cent of the exposed cells died; with three consecutive 20-minute sessions, between 65 and 70 per cent died. The scientists from the University of California San Diego also noticed mutations with the same patterns as those seen in skin cancer patients.

Again, though, we should bear in mind that cells in a lab are more vulnerable to damage than the skin cells on our hands – and the authors noted themselves that a long-term study would be needed before we can conclusively determine whether these devices lead to an increased skin cancer risk.

open image in gallery Dermatologists recommend avoiding at-home kits and heading to a professional instead ( Getty/iStock )

“The evidence specifically linking UV nail lamps to skin cancer remains limited,” Dr Phillips says. “Current research suggests that prolonged and repeated exposure may pose a low risk, although the available evidence is weak. As UV damage is cumulative, I would still recommend minimising unnecessary exposure, particularly for people who have gel manicures frequently.”

To do so, he suggests applying “a high factor, broad spectrum SPF to the hands before a gel manicure, or wearing dark, opaque fingerless gloves” – it probably makes sense to pop these on before any polish is applied, just to avoid smudges.

Other ingredients to be wary of are acrylates, which help to bond the varnish to your nail for that long-lasting finish; one of the most popular is known as HEMA, short for hydroxyethyl methacrylate. “When the gel is placed under a UV or LED lamp, these chemicals react to form the hard, durable coating of a gel manicure,” Dr Phillips says.

open image in gallery Chemicals react to the UV or LED lamp to produce the durable nail coating ( Getty/iStock )

Acrylates like HEMA have caused concern because they can trigger allergic contact dermatitis, a skin condition that results in painful, itchy, dry skin around the fingers and nails, and potentially on the eyelids and face. It can also cause swelling, which might prompt the nail plate to loosen from its bed.

In 2018, the British Association of Dermatologists warned that acrylates were causing a spike in contact dermatitis tantamount to an “epidemic”, with an estimated 2.4 per cent of people affected. And a few years later, in 2023, the Office for Product Safety and Standards launched a formal investigation.

Once you’ve become sensitised, future contact with these chemicals might trigger a reaction again

The problem arises when uncured varnish containing acrylates comes into contact with the skin and triggers an immune response. This is more likely to happen when the product isn’t applied properly, whether that’s by amateurs using at-home kits or by salon staff who haven’t been properly trained.

There are “wider implications”, Dr Phillips says, because acrylates are “also used in some dental materials, medical adhesives and the bone cement used in certain orthopaedic procedures, including joint replacements”. Once you’ve become sensitised, future contact with these chemicals might trigger a reaction again – so you could be setting yourself up for a lifetime of issues.

Products containing HEMA aren’t banned outright, but they are restricted to professional use. An at-home gel kit, then, should already use HEMA-free polish – but dermatologists and manicurists tend to recommend that you sidestep these altogether and just see a qualified professional.

It’s important, Dr Phillips adds, “to avoid getting gel on the surrounding skin and to make sure the product is fully hardened under the appropriate lamp” – sometimes the lamps in bargain kits are lower wattage, and won’t properly harden the gel.

Essentially, he says, “occasional gel manicures are unlikely to pose a significant health risk for most people”. But if you’re getting a new set of gels every few weeks or so, it’s definitely worth asking your technician about the products they’re using, and taking precautions wherever you can. Sure, fingerless gloves might not be the most fashionable accompaniment to your manicure, but skin health is never going to go out of style.

The history of music is littered with the detritus of Hollywood’s vanity. Many an A-list actor has convinced themselves they’ve got the goods to make it as a musician, be that Eddie Murphy, Bruce Willis, or Robert Downey Jr. The results are seldom good. To this end, you might have reason to hoist an eyebrow when you spot Sir Anthony Hopkins is releasing an album this week. But how wrong you’d be.

Life is a Dream is the second record from the Oscar-winning star of The Silence of the Lambs and The Father. (His previous album, Composer, was released on CD in 2012, through Classic FM.) Those who might be bewildered by the mental image of the 88-year-old Welshman strutting a stage like Mick Jagger singing “Sympathy for the Devil” need not worry: these are classical compositions, composed by Hopkins over the course of his life and performed by the Philharmonia Orchestra with Grammy Award-winning conductor Gustavo Dudamel.

There is something wonderfully, life-affirmingly sweet about this music, which shifts between classical forms, from bright, brass-led fanfares to elegant waltzes. It would be easy to sound patronising about Hopkins’s passion project, were it not for the fact that it is legitimately good. There is more music artistry on show here than in many of today’s charting pop releases – albeit in service of a genre that gets scant shrift in the mainstream. Hopkins has a pleasing grasp of harmony and an ear for flighty melody; in the spectrum of classical music, it’s on the more traditional side, absent of the dissonance and tonal complexity that the 20th century brought to the genre.

Life is a Dream is a personal thing for Hopkins; that much is evident in the music’s wordless sentimentality. Some of the tracks are inspired by his native Wales, including “1947: Suite for Solo Piano and Orchestra: II. Bracken Road”, which he wrote in 1963 while working as a young actor at the Liverpool Playhouse. Hopkins began learning the piano at the age of four, and has written music since he was a child, describing music as “my first desire” and “my first wish”. Several of his compositions have been performed before in concert halls around the world; renowned conductor André Rieu recorded a waltz by Hopkins on his 2011 album And the Waltz Goes On; that work also features here.

From ‘Elephant Man’ to music man: Anthony Hopkins in the studio ( Charlie Gray )

To some extent, hearing Hopkins’s music simply confirms what everyone has always known about him. Whatever the project – even while playing sociopathic cannibal Hannibal Lecter in The Silence of the Lambs – he radiates sophistication and sincerity. On some level, it simply makes sense that Hopkins is able to compose such moving, edifying music: it’s an extension of what he’s been doing his whole career.

When a wealthy celebrity, respected in their field, decides to venture out and try their hand in another, it’s hard to escape the whiff of egocentrism. We do not expect these things to be good, or particularly meaningful; they are referred to as “side projects” for a reason. It’s a credit both to Hopkins’ craft and his judgement that such dismissals fall away while actually listening to Life is a Dream. It is honest music made for the right reasons. In a way, he can be as proud of this as he can of any of his screen performances – and he probably is.

What’s more, for Hopkins to do this at 88 is nothing short of inspirational. If there’s a lesson here, it’s that life doesn’t stop when you hit 60, or 70, or 80. (Or even when you become the oldest actor to ever win an Oscar, at the age of 83.) There’s always something more to do. There’s always more music, waiting to be played.

‘Life is a Dream’ is out now on Decca Classics

Asian shares were mixed on Friday following a retreat on Wall Street as a U.S. Treasury Department plan to boost its government debt buybacks had only limited capacity to calm markets.

U.S. futures edged higher.

Japan’s Nikkei 225 fell 0.2% to 66,080.25. South Korea’s Kospi climbed 0.9% to 6,914.09. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng added 0.7% to 25,888.36, while the Shanghai Composite index was unchanged at 3,903.81.

Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 was trading 0.3% lower at 9,053.90. Taiwan’s Taiex gained 0.4%, while India’s Sensex was 0.1% lower.

The Treasury Department announced Wednesday that it will at least double the size of its planned purchases of longer-term government debt, while Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent signaled Thursday that the repurchase program could be larger.

The announcement temporarily brought down government bond yields, which have been elevated under concerns about high inflation partly caused by the war in Iran and rising U.S. government debt. Higher yields tend to slow the broader economy due to increased borrowing costs across the financial system and can undercut stock prices.

But analysts said they expect the effect on bond yields were to be temporary. The yield of the U.S. 10-year Treasury was at around 4.71% early Friday, up from nearly 4.64% on Thursday and back to around the level before the Treasury department’s announcement.

The 30-year Treasury yield was at about 5.26%, up from 5.18% on Thursday.

In Asia, bond yields also rose back. Japan’s 10-year government bond yield, which had been trading near 30-year highs, rose to 2.88% from around 2.83% on Thursday.

The latest climb in bond yields has weighed on share prices. On Thursday, Wall Street’s benchmark S&P 500 lost 0.9%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.3%, and the technology-heavy Nasdaq composite dropped 1%.

In other dealings early Friday, oil prices fell slightly, even as the U.S. stepped up its economic threats toward Iran while limited progress has been made toward de-escalation of tensions between Washington and Tehran.

Brent crude, the international standard, fell 0.2% to $93.64 a barrel. It was trading at roughly $72 per barrel before the start of the war. Benchmark U.S. crude was down 0.3% to $86.59 a barrel.

The U.S. dollar fell to 159.01 Japanese yen from 159.05 yen. The euro was trading at $1.1694, up from $1.1678.

A Swiss tourist has been sentenced to a year in prison in Bali for posting videos boasting that he had broken the rules of Nyepi, the Balinese day of silence, and calling the tradition crazy.

Luzian Andrin Zgraggen, 26, was convicted at the Denpasar district court on Thursday of insulting a religious observance under Indonesia's new criminal code. The court found he had made the posts after staff at the villa where he was staying explained the restrictions to him.

"What the defendant did offended the Balinese people, hurt their faith and provoked public outrage," said presiding judge, Tjokorda Putra Budi Pastima, according to the Associated Press. "The defendant must be held accountable for his actions."

Nyepi, marking the Balinese new year, fell on 19 March this year.

To observe the day, nobody leaves their home or accommodation for 24 hours, except in an emergency. The beaches and streets remain empty apart from patrols enforcing the silence. The island's airport closes and the internet is switched off.

Entertainment is restricted, even the use of electricity is discouraged, and residents stock up on food beforehand so they can stay indoors. The rules apply to everyone on the island whatever their religion or nationality.

Mr Zgraggen filmed himself walking to an empty beach during the observance, smiling at the camera, and in one clip called the scene crazy while swearing in the caption. The video, since removed, was widely reshared and drew anger from Balinese residents. Police traced him after public complaints and arrested him in March at a villa in Legian, a tourist area near Kuta beach.

Hindu devotees pray during the Melasti ceremony prayer at Kenjeran beach in Surabaya on March 14, 2026. Melasti is a purification festival which is held several days before "Nyepi", the day of silence, when Hindu devotees are not allowed to work, travel or take part in any indulgence ( AFP/Getty )

He told the court, in a trial that began in June, that he had never meant to insult the holiday or the Balinese people, and that he made the posts while hungry and frustrated at being unable to get food during the shutdown, without fully understanding how far the restrictions went.

"I deeply regret what I did, I apologise to the Balinese people," he said in his defence plea, according to AP.

Tourists, both foreign and Indonesian, have been detained or deported before for going outside during Nyepi, but those cases were generally settled without prosecution.

Bali received a record seven million foreign visitors last year, well above its pre-pandemic numbers, and the return of mass tourism has brought complaints from residents about the behaviour of some of them. Foreigners have been penalised for offensive acts at religious sites, for flouting traffic laws and for setting up enclaves that exclude locals, and the authorities have promised tighter scrutiny of visitors and a crackdown on those who misbehave.

Bali is a predominantly Hindu island in Indonesia, which has the largest Muslim population of any country.

News.title: Charter plane with eight people on board crashes near remote Alaska radar station

Heavy rain and winds pounded the Northeast U.S. on Thursday as storms tore through a beach on Long Island, stranded dozens of people in their cars in New Jersey and knocked out power in parts of Delaware's capital city.

Photos and video shared on social media show debris thrown in the air and pummeling rain as a possible tornado touched down at Atlantic Beach on Long Island’s outer barrier. It tore apart a major beach club, leaving broken beach chairs and wood beams littered across the shoreline.

Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman said there were no reports of serious injuries or deaths, but there had been damage to property and a search team was making sure no one was trapped in the cabanas. He declared a state of emergency.

“There are reports of people trapped in their vehicles due to flooding in the south shore, and first responders are assisting in their rescue,” he said in a statement.

The Sun and Surf Beach Club said buildings had been significantly damaged and it temporarily closed that club and nearby Silver Point.

The National Weather Service had warned of waterspouts, tornado-like hazards that happen over water, in the area but wasn’t able to immediately confirm a tornado on the beach.

Bryan Ramsey, a meteorologist for the weather service in New York, said the storm was moving East offshore Thursday evening and was expected to taper over the next several hours.

In other parts of New York, flooding caused part of the Long Island Expressway in Queens to close in both directions, according to New York City Emergency Management. Photos on social media showed lines of stopped cars as emergency crews traversed the water.

In Jersey City, New Jersey, emergency crews rescued 69 people trapped in cars that had been overtaken by flash flooding Thursday, said Mayor James Solomon. Emergency crews waded through roads with knee-high water with small inflatable boats to help those stranded.

A likely tornado touched down in Dover, Delaware, and caused significant damage across the city, the police department reported. There were no reports of serious injuries, police said.

“Dover — please take this seriously. Stay home. Stay safe,” the department said on Facebook.

Photos and video online show fallen trees, downed power lines and flooded roads.

The Delaware Electric Cooperative said more than 1,000 customers didn’t have power in the northern part of its service area, but within a few hours most of the outages had been fixed.

News.title: Brook falls agonisingly short of Headingley hundred again as England continue to dominate
News.content:
“Yeah, of course I did,” said Cox, when asked if he was frustrated to miss out on three figures. Cox was caught behind off spinner Ali Usman, but believed he had hit his pad with his bat, not the ball.

“Once I got to fifty, I moved to sixty quickly, and thought ‘there’s a chance here’. Just keep being disciplined, ball by ball. I had it at the back of my mind, thinking you have worked so hard, do not give this opportunity up. That is exactly what I do in county cricket. I get to fifty, see how many runs I need to score, and work down from there.”

Asked if his team-mates were feeling the same emotion, he said: “Oh yeah there is. Every team, every player wants to score Test hundreds. Four of us got fifties, so we were hoping one would kick on, and instead of making it just a hundred, make it 150 or 170.

“I am thrilled. I would have taken it at the start of the Test match. I let myself down a tiny bit, but at the end of the day, you take 70.”

Cox resumed on day two on 23, then was dropped by the bowler Khurram Shahzad on 57. In the course of his innings, he was compared to AB de Villiers by the former England captain Michael Vaughan.

Cox is likely to get a good run across formats. England had hoped to call on Sam Curran for the third Test of this series, but his summer is over due to a groin injury. Curran will undergo surgery on Friday.

It is likely England will be without Curran, Bethell and Tom Banton for September’s white-ball series against Sri Lanka, which should mean greater opportunity for the likes of Cox and Sussex’s James Coles, and could even see a recall for Zak Crawley, who made an assured 81 for Kent against Middlesex on Thursday. Will Jacks is currently sidelined with appendicitis, but is expected to have recovered in time for the series.

News.title: Robinson demolishes Pakistan to cement importance to new regime
News.content:
He also has that edge, the grunt of an angry fast bowler, and his competitiveness was just what Root needed considering his other quicks were still in Hundred mode. Archer bowled too short, Gus Atkinson grew into the innings but was wicketless and it took a while for Tongue to click, although once he did he was unplayable against the right-handers with his pace and angle.

Robinson’s lack of pace gives them the keeper-standing-up option. It worked a treat when he bowled Pakistan’s top-scorer, Abdullah Shafique for 61, his footwork messed up by Jamie Smith breathing down his neck.

Pakistan would have batted first had they won the toss and it is a good pitch that will improve as the Test goes on, although with rain around all week the overheads will have a say on the game. Pakistan have far more recent red-ball exposure than England’s batsmen but they were ill-equipped to deal with Robinson and Tongue.

Most supporters were still walking into the ground when the former struck first ball, Azan Awais lbw to a nip-backer. Shan Masood’s stilted footwork was ripe for exposing and Robinson’s first ball over the wicket to the left-hander was full and straight to beat the loose drive.

Imam-ul-Haq had done the hard work, seeing off Robinson only to flash a drive to second slip off a wide ball from Tongue to end Pakistan’s only stand of substance of the innings: 93 for the third wicket.

Robinson cracked the innings open further with Saud Shakeel leg before, who was too slow to call for the review that would have saved him. Hawk-Eye showed the ball would have gone over the top.

Robinson then bowled Shafique in his next over and Pakistan were toppling. Tongue cranked up the pace, bowled full and the perpendicular angle into the right-handers did the rest.

News.title: Burnham blames Trump’s war in Iran for higher inflation
News.content:
Andy Burnham has blamed Donald Trump’s war in Iran for higher inflation in Britain.

Inflation jumped from 2.6pc in June to 2.9pc last month, according to the Office for National Statistics, threatening to undermine Mr Burnham’s pledge to bring down the cost of living.

The Prime Minister said: “We can’t control though what is going on in the Middle East and the effect of the conflict there is now being felt in inflation here, and in other countries around the world.

“I realise these times are really hard but already people can see a month into office I have done things that will make a difference.”

July’s inflation figure was affected by a 13.5pc rise in the Ofgem price cap in response to the energy crisis unleashed by the Iran war. It means prices are now rising at their highest rate since March.

The latest figure shows the struggle that Mr Burnham faces to fulfil his promise to bring down living costs.

There are fears that inflation will climb higher in the coming months as the impact of the conflict filters through to the economy.

Speaking at an event in the North East, Mr Burnham added: “I want to lead a cost-of-living Government, and I’ve already taken steps as Prime Minister to show I will help people wherever I can. I can’t do everything, I think people know that.

“We’re in tough times, but where I can do something to make life that little bit better, I will do it.”

Since arriving in No 10, Mr Burnham has made tackling the cost of living a key policy focus.

The Prime Minister announced last month that he would remove VAT from electricity bills from October and reinstate the £2 cap on bus fares from next year.

However, average energy bills are expected to jump by around 4pc from October, according to energy analysts Cornwall Insight, wiping out any potential savings from Mr Burnham’s VAT cut.

The analysts said Ofgem’s price cap – which limits the average annual energy bill faced by a family home – would rise from £1,663 to £1,729.

Despite concerns about increasing gas and electricity bills, July’s rate of inflation was in line with economists’ expectations.

Money markets now expect policymakers at the Bank of England to hold interest rates at 3.75pc at their next meeting in September.

News.title: Unemployment rate fails to fall for Burnham
News.content:
An expected drop in the unemployment rate has failed to materialise, dealing a setback to Andy Burnham’s hopes of reviving Britain’s ailing economy.

Unemployment remained stuck at 4.9pc in the three months to June, while the number of payrolled employees fell by 13,000, according to figures from the Office for National Statistics. Economists had predicted that the unemployment rate would ease to 4.8pc.

While the three-month figure was flat, monthly data showed a sharp increase at the end of the period. Unemployment jumped to 5.4pc in June, up from 4.6pc the previous month.

That marked the highest reading since October 2020 and the biggest monthly jump in 13 years.

Julian Jessop, at the Institute of Economic Affairs, described the latest jobs figures as “dire”.

He said: “The unemployment rate remains stubbornly high, with a big jump in the single month figure for June.”

It came as private sector wage growth slumped to a six-year low of just 2.8pc. That stands in contrast to a 6.1pc pay increase for the average public sector worker in the same period.

Meanwhile, vacancies dropped to 707,000 in the three months to July – the lowest level since 2021 – with a particular strain on entry-level job openings.

Ben Harrison, director of the Work Foundation at Lancaster University, warned that the UK was “trapped in a deepening jobs drought”.

Thomas Pugh, chief economist at RSM UK, said: “Stagnant, or even negative, real wage growth in the second half of this year will intensify the pressure on Burnham and Healey to come up with a package to support the cost of living.

“However, doing anything substantial without breaching either the fiscal rules or the manifesto commitments looks increasingly difficult given the deterioration in headroom and commitments to spend big on everything from defence to social care.”

Sports.content:
Arsenal 'exploring Kenan Yildiz transfer' with chance of completing blockbuster swap

Arsenal still want to sign a forward after missing out on Real Madrid's Vinicius Junior and new Chelsea signing Morgan Rogers, with Mikel Arteta especially keen on Kenan Yildiz

View 2 Images Kenan Yildiz is valued at £60million by Juventus (Image: Filippo Alfero - Juventus FC/Juventus FC via Getty Images)

Arsenal are exploring a move for Juventus star Kenan Yildiz in a deal which could see Gabriel Martinelli go the other way. Yildiz, 21, is high on the Gunners' shortlist and Mikel Arteta in particular wants the German-born Turkey international.

‌



Having agreed a £51million deal to sign Ezri Konsa and in turn alleviate their defensive concerns, Arsenal's focus has switched to signing a forward, particularly one who can play on the left wing. The Gunners were interested in Morgan Rogers before his £117million move to Chelsea and missed out on Vinicius Junior after he decided to extend his contract with Real Madrid.

‌



Now, according to the Independent, Yildiz is being targeted. Juventus would demand north of £60m, a fee which would take Arsenal's net spend this summer to almost £200m after paying sums for Christos Tzolis, Bruno Guimaraes and soon enough Konsa.

‌



So, a solution to help balance the books has been discussed. It's reported that although negotiations would be required, Martinelli could be used in a swap deal, with the 25-year-old having been left out of Arteta's squad for the Community Shield.

FOLLOW OUR ARSENAL FB PAGE! Latest Gunners news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

‌



Yildiz signed for Juventus on a free transfer in the summer of 2022 after coming through Bayern Munich's academy. The 21-year-old enjoyed by far his most productive campaign last season, scoring 11 goals and providing nine assists in 47 appearances, although Juventus could only manage a sixth-place finish in Serie A.

Meanwhile, some thought at Arsenal has been given to waiting until future windows to sign Junior Kroupi from Bournemouth, who was a target prior to his pre-season injury. Julian Alvarez also remains on Arsenal's shortlist and there's a possibility that Atletico Madrid's refusal to sell him to Barcelona, coupled with his desire to leave, could yet present an opportunity for the Gunners.

Arteta has made it clear both privately and in public that Arsenal can't stand still after winning the Premier League title, with their next aim being to lift the Champions League and get their hands on domestic trophies. "Well, we are really active in the market. I think I mentioned that a few days ago," he said on Thursday when asked about their pursuit of Konsa.

‌



"The ambition is to improve the squad. We have a really specific issue in the backline, especially with the long-term injury of Wilo [Saliba] and the fact that we miss one more defender; that's clear. So we are trying to reinforce that area. Whenever we're ready, we'll announce something."

Should Arsenal swap Gabriel Martinelli for Kenan Yildiz? Have your say in the comments section.

View 2 Images Gabriel Martinelli's future at Arsenal remains uncertain (Image: Marc Atkins/Getty Images)

‌



Arteta went on to admit that some long-serving players such as Martinelli may have to be moved on in order to accommodate new signings. "It's a really, really tough moment, you need to face that reality," he confessed.

"But you need to face it with real honesty and transparency because when you are on the other side, that's exactly what you need. You might not like what you've been told, but if it's truthful, if it's the reality, if it's honest and it's going to help you to make better decisions and have more clarity for the next steps in your career, you have to do that.

"These are always very difficult conversations, but they need to be done. It's like when a player doesn't feel that he belongs or he's important, he wants to have a different chapter, I think that communication has to exist and it has to be both ways.

Article continues below

"We all know, everything has a start and has an end. When it comes to the end, I think our duty, our responsibility is to do it in the best possible way, maintaining the respect and admiration for the player and the relationship, but understanding that at the end, we need to make football decisions."

United are set to receive an unexpected gift in the transfer window, with former defender Willy Kambwala all set to leave Villarreal. The 21-year-old made 10 appearances for United before joining the Spanish club in 2024.

‌



View 3 Images Kambwala left United in 2024 (Image: Getty)

The Manchester Evening News reports that United included a "sizeable" sell-on fee when dealing with Villarreal two years ago. Italian club Como are claimed to be leading the race for Kambwala's signature, while La Liga club Osasuna have also shown interest.

The situation means United will receive a small sum when Kambwala leaves Villarreal, as he is not expected to command a significant fee, which reduces the amount heading back to Old Trafford. The defender has made 23 total appearances since leaving United, with injury limiting his minutes last season.

‌
