Nika Gvaramia interview

World.title: Opinion: ‘Removing Kobakhidze would be logical move for Ivanishvili if prime minister does not move against him first’
World.content:
Opinion on Georgian Prime Minister Kobakhidze

According to Eka Gigauri, executive director of Transparency International Georgia, removing Prime Minister Kobakhidze could eventually become a logical step for Ivanishvili — provided the prime minister does not manage to seize political power himself.

Eka Gigauri: “The Garibashvili case has once again confirmed what we already knew:”

None of this has anything to do with fighting corruption. Ivanishvili is reshuffling his inner circle, while Kobakhidze — with his approval and Mdinaradze’s assistance — is getting rid of political rivals. In “Georgian Dream”, no one is surprised when people enrich themselves at the public’s expense or engage in corruption: they all steal. The entire system is built on corruption, and Ivanishvili gave them the freedom to do so. So the “fight against corruption” is merely a staged performance designed to conceal a settling of scores. Kobakhidze does not get his hands dirty himself. He has Mdinaradze to do that for him, who has become his loyal executor and servant. It is obvious that the overwhelming majority of “Georgian Dream” supporters genuinely support Garibashvili. The same cannot be said of Kobakhidze and Mdinaradze. Look at the reactions from “Dream” supporters to statements by Garibashvili and his wife. If the authorities imprisoned Mdinaradze and then Kobakhidze, “Dream” supporters would not say a word in their defence. To them, Kobakhidze is still a former NGO worker and employee of international organisations. He is not a churchgoer and has no particular ties to the Church. The same applies to much of his team. There is no friendship, brotherhood or willingness to support one another in the “Georgian Dream” party. Apparently, none of them possesses that quintessential Georgian sense of honour. Out of fear of Bidzina, and now of Kobakhidze as well, they will betray one another, throw each other under the bus and abandon one another in times of trouble. Ivanishvili is deliberately deepening divisions within his own team and turning its members against one another. His goal is to prevent them from uniting against him and to force them to constantly undermine and confront each other. Today, Kobakhidze is clearly Ivanishvili’s favourite. However, he appears to have been carried away by this status. He often talks about his personal achievements, as though he had the power to act even without Ivanishvili. He may not have many genuine supporters within “Georgian Dream”, but today he exercises almost complete control over state institutions. “Georgian Dream” members appear to fear Kobakhidze greatly — perhaps even more than Bidzina. They know that Kobakhidze has direct access to Bidzina and can tell him something about a fellow party member that could ultimately destroy them. Even Garibashvili did not have this kind of influence. Kobakhidze has placed his people almost everywhere, while parliament is under his complete control. He has gradually concentrated enormous power in his hands. If this continues, even Ivanishvili may find it difficult to dismantle the system.

The experience of authoritarian regimes around the world also shows that dictators manage their inner circles according to the principle of “divide and rule”. They periodically replace their favourites and involve everyone in corruption schemes and other crimes, so that they can later use their weaknesses and complicity against them. At the same time, they pit influential groups against one another and keep everyone in a constant state of fear through selective punishment.

Thus, no individual or group can accumulate enough power to pose a real threat to the leader. However, such a system also carries a significant risk: a favourite who has concentrated all the levers of power in their hands may eventually begin building an independent political force. That is why dictators often get rid of their most loyal and influential allies.

At the same time, members of an authoritarian ruler’s inner circle often initiate changes of power. In other words, autocrats and dictators have good reason to fear their own inner circles. Today, if Kobakhidze wanted to, he could even remove Bidzina, and no one in “Georgian Dream” would dare oppose him. Therefore, removing Kobakhidze would eventually become a perfectly logical step — unless he managed to remove Ivanishvili first.

Opinion on Georgian Prime Minister Kobakhidze

World.title: ‘We are not on our knees, we are fighting for justice’: David Babayan’s message from Baku prison
World.content:
David Babayan’s message from a Baku prison

“What kind of trial was it? It was a theatrical performance, with the script written in advance,” David Babayan, the former foreign minister of the former unrecognised Nagorno-Karabakh Republic, said in a message from a Baku prison.

Babayan’s family gave the audio recording of his message to an Armenian media outlet. In his message, he discusses the trial of the former NKR’s military and political leadership. Two weeks ago, the Court of Appeal upheld the verdicts handed down by the Baku Military Court. In February 2026, David Babayan received a life sentence. He described the Court of Appeal’s ruling as a “formal stage” that had to be completed before the case could be taken to an international court.

“One interesting development was that one of the defence lawyers here [at the Baku court] said they did not want the case to reach an international court because more than 95% of the charges were fabricated and there was no evidence. That is exactly what happened,” Babayan said.

He also said that he and other prisoners were facing serious health problems. He stressed that despite their difficult situation, they were fighting for justice, freedom and human rights.

“It is one thing to fight and stand up for justice, and another to sit in prison for it. But know this: although we are imprisoned, we are not on our knees,” Babayan concluded.

On 5 February 2026, the Baku Military Court sentenced former president Arayik Harutyunyan, Defence Army commander Levon Mnatsakanyan, deputy commander Davit Manukyan, parliament speaker Davit Ishkhanyan and foreign minister David Babayan to life imprisonment. The court sentenced former presidents Arkady Ghukasyan and Bako Sahakyan to 20 years in prison. Baku brought serious charges against all the defendants, ranging from terrorism to genocide. The two former presidents received shorter sentences because of their age. Under Azerbaijani law, courts cannot sentence people over 65 to life imprisonment. The case of former state minister Ruben Vardanyan was heard separately. On 17 February, a Baku court sentenced him to 20 years in prison.

Falsifications instead of evidence

“Remarkably, instead of evidence, they use substitutes here: lies, falsifications, toasts, various political approaches, slogans and so on.

We pointed out that the legal system and the courts cannot operate like the food or chemical industries, where people use substitutes.

Nothing can replace facts and evidence.

But that is how things work in this court. And that is their general approach to us.

Moreover, these falsifications and lies remain in their archives. At times, we tried to see how they recorded all this in their documents. We found that they had not included our statements at all or, at best, had included heavily shortened or distorted versions. This is nothing other than legal apartheid.”

On the old and new charges against him

“What is happening here is simply unimaginable. For example, they automatically attribute a crime committed by one person to everyone.

They added two life-sentence charges to my case that had never appeared before and had never been mentioned throughout the entire first-instance trial. I noticed this when they gave us a brief summary a week after the trial ended. This is unacceptable.

I asked them to review our statements — both my final statement at the first-instance trial and the main statements we made during this trial — and provide them in video format to Azerbaijan’s human rights ombudsman. But they refused.

They say the trial is open, but refuse to provide all the information even to their own human rights ombudsman.

One interesting phenomenon was that five or six defence lawyers changed during this period. One of them changed at the very beginning of the appeal proceedings. I tried to find out why. They told me it was because of health problems. During the hearing, I said: ‘Contact him by video. I want to ask him about his health personally.’ Of course, they became uncomfortable and did not put us in contact. They said his life was not in danger.

They sentenced me to life imprisonment under an article alleging that I had tried to seize power here [in Azerbaijan] and overthrow the constitutional order.

I asked whether there was any evidence that I had taken part in a struggle for power while I was here. If that were the case, I would have had supporters across your country and cells belonging to some organisation. Of course, I received no answer.

The court accepted 100% of our complaints in favour of the prosecution. At the first-instance trial, 99.4% of them went in favour of the prosecution.

I thanked them for mistakes of such quality and quantity because they are very important for us. They will help justice prevail because we will present all of this to an international court.”

Selected groups of people were brought to the hearings on special buses

“There were no Azerbaijani citizens at the Court of Appeal hearings, whereas the first-instance trial always had around 200-300 people in attendance.

Of course, they selected all of them specifically and brought them in on special buses. We saw this.

According to some reports, they were also paid well. But no one attended this trial.

One reason is that these people saw the abuses that took place there. They saw the weak position of their own side, our independent defence, our persistence and the quality of our self-defence. Naturally, whether they wanted it or not, all this information reached their society. That is why they banned these people from attending.”

David Babayan’s message from a Baku prison

World.title: A Gal-Media TV station building has burned down in Abkhazia
World.content:
In Abkhazia, a building housing the regional TV company Gal-Media has been destroyed by fire. Without their equipment, journalists now plan to film their reports using smartphones.

The TV company, which serves the predominantly ethnic Georgian Gali district, occupied several rooms in a four-storey building. The fire destroyed the editing room, recording room and studio where the main news bulletins were produced. It also destroyed all the studio equipment, the server room and the entire archive.

Security camera footage helped investigators identify the exact point where the fire started. It broke out near the ceiling, where a layer of soundproofing foam had been installed. Specialists believe an old bundle of electrical wiring may have caused the fire. Although the premises underwent renovations in 2016, workers did not replace this old section of wiring.

Gali district administration head Konstantin Pilia said emergency services were investigating the incident and expected to release their findings in the coming days. Specialists are also assessing the extent of the damage and the cost of repairs and replacement equipment. The district and republican authorities have already begun taking steps to restore the TV station’s operations.

Because of the fire, Gal-Media will continue operating on a limited basis. Journalists will temporarily use their surviving personal smartphones and laptops to prepare reports. This will allow them to publish information on social media. However, the station’s regular analogue broadcasts will be suspended for the time being, Gal-Media head Thea Arshba said.

The Gali district administration is already looking for temporary premises for the TV company’s staff while repairs are under way.

World.title: From C5 to C6: how Azerbaijan is reshaping balance of power in Central Asia
World.content:
Azerbaijan at Central Asia’s table

On 16 November 2025, the five Central Asian states accepted Azerbaijan as a full member of the Consultative Meeting of Heads of State. Eight months later, on 31 July, Ilham Aliyev took his place at the table at an informal summit in Cholpon-Ata not as a guest, but as one of six equal participants.

The format is now officially known as “Central Asia and Azerbaijan”. The term “C6” has already entered expert vocabulary and is being used at conferences.

The change expands Central Asia’s political and economic cooperation to the western shore of the Caspian Sea. It also turns Azerbaijan from an external partner into a full participant in a route connecting the region with Turkey and Europe.

How did the format emerge and why has it expanded?

Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev proposed the idea of a consultative mechanism at the UN in September 2017. The first meeting took place in Astana on 15 March 2018. The format’s advantage was its simplicity: without a treaty, permanent secretariat or supranational bodies, the leaders of the five countries could directly discuss borders, water resources, trade and security.

Azerbaijan did not join the process immediately. Ilham Aliyev attended meetings in Dushanbe in 2023, Astana in 2024 and Tashkent in 2025 as an honorary guest. Since the beginning of 2023, he has visited Central Asian countries 16 times, while the region’s leaders have travelled to Azerbaijan 26 times. In 2025, Azerbaijan’s trade with the five Central Asian states grew by 53% to $1.8 billion. Trade among the Central Asian countries themselves reached $10.7 billion in 2024.

Mirziyoyev described Baku’s accession as an opportunity to create a “single space for cooperation” between Central Asia and the South Caucasus. Aliyev, in turn, described the two shores of the Caspian as a “single geopolitical and geoeconomic space”.

The leaders of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan said they supported expanding the format because it would create new opportunities for transit, logistics and energy cooperation.

The Middle Corridor and the Caspian’s role in bringing the region together

The geography offers the clearest explanation for Azerbaijan’s participation in the format. The Middle Corridor links China and Central Asia with Europe: goods travel by rail across Kazakhstan to the ports of Aktau and Kuryk, then across the Caspian Sea to Alat, before continuing through Georgia towards Turkey and the Black Sea. Azerbaijan effectively serves as the western gateway to the route.

According to the Kazakh government, freight volumes along the Trans-Caspian route rose by 62% in 2024 to 4.5 million tonnes. Baku says the volume of cargo travelling through the Azerbaijani section of the Middle Corridor has increased by 90% over three years. The authorities plan to raise the capacity of the Port of Alat to 25 million tonnes a year. The World Bank estimates that if countries coordinate border procedures, tariffs, port operations and transport schedules, freight volumes along the corridor could triple by 2030, while delivery times could fall by half.

The plans go beyond container shipping. Proposed electricity and digital cable projects across the Caspian would also bring energy and information flows into the broader agenda of regional cooperation.

The route through Nakhchivan offers new opportunities but remains contentious. The Washington Declaration, signed on 8 August 2025, provides for a transport link through Armenia between mainland Azerbaijan and Nakhchivan, based on the sovereignty and jurisdiction of the states concerned, as well as the development of the TRIPP mechanism. Baku calls the route the “Zangezur Corridor”.

If implemented, the route could give the Middle Corridor an additional link to Turkey. However, until the parties agree on customs procedures, security arrangements, financing and management mechanisms, it remains a project rather than an operational transport corridor.

What is changing from a geopolitical perspective?

“C6” is a convenient political label, not the official name of an organisation. The format remains a consultative platform based on consensus. It does not involve collective defence commitments or mechanisms to enforce decisions.

For Moscow, this is therefore primarily about competition over logistics and political influence, including through the development of routes that bypass Russia, rather than the emergence of a new military alliance.

Beijing gains an additional route to the west and more stable conditions for transit.

Ankara has an interest in strengthening direct transport links across the Caspian.

The European Union and the US see the format as an opportunity to reduce dependence on routes through Russia and expand access to Central Asia.

The new C6 format should not be confused with the Organisation of Turkic States. The OTS has a treaty-based framework and institutional cooperation among Turkic states. The “Central Asia and Azerbaijan” format also includes Tajikistan and focuses less on shared identity than on geography, economic interests and regional cooperation.

Potential opportunities and real constraints

The potential areas for cooperation are quite concrete: common transit tariffs, digital customs procedures, coordinated port and railway schedules, joint investment funds, green energy exports, tourism routes and coordination at international forums. With its ports, financial resources and transport links through the Caucasus and Turkey, Azerbaijan offers Central Asian countries additional routes and opportunities. Baku, in turn, gains more systematic access to the region’s five markets and their economic ties with China.

However, there are also many constraints. The six countries differ in their economic potential, interests in water resources and energy, and priorities in their relations with Russia, China, Turkey and the West. The format has no permanent secretariat or mechanisms to enforce decisions, so implementation of political agreements will depend on intergovernmental coordination.

The Convention on the Legal Status of the Caspian Sea, signed in 2018, has yet to be ratified by Iran, while delimiting the seabed requires separate agreements. Falling water levels in the Caspian, the shallowing of ports and the need for costly dredging also increase the environmental and economic costs of transport logistics.

From symbol to concrete projects?

Mirziyoyev has already proposed transforming the format into a “Community of Central Asia” with a rotating secretariat. The next official meeting, scheduled for 8 October 2026 in Avaza, will be one of the first tests of whether these intentions can turn into practical decisions.

Will the six countries agree on common tariffs, digital customs procedures and a stable ferry schedule? Will TRIPP become a fully fledged part of the Middle Corridor without creating new border disputes? Or will the “Central Asia and Azerbaijan” format remain a flexible consultative platform, with its informal nature continuing to be its main advantage?

Azerbaijan at Central Asia’s table

World.title: Convicted former Georgian PM Garibashvili: ‘Authorities left me no choice, I have to fight’
World.content:
Letter from Georgia’s former prime minister from prison

Convicted former Georgian prime minister Irakli Garibashvili says in a letter published from prison that the authorities arrested him to end his political career. He also says he gave up his legal fight to avoid a confrontation with the authorities.

The former prime minister writes that he received a letter from Regional Development Minister Mamuka Mdinaradze in July. According to Garibashvili, he confirmed to Mdinaradze that same day that he did not intend to return to politics.

Mamuka Mdinaradze’s press office has described Garibashvili’s claims as “complete absurdity”.

“I state with full responsibility that I did everything to avoid confrontation with the [ruling] team and with someone who is dear to me,” Garibashvili wrote.

He says this is why he abandoned his legal challenge and went through the entire process to the end — to avoid, as he put it, harming the interests of the state and the “team”.

“Unfortunately, in response I received a staged dirty provocation, a sea of lies and injustice. Throughout this time, the public heard not a single word from me. I endured this ordeal patiently,” Garibashvili said.

According to Garibashvili, despite the position he had expressed to Mdinaradze, the authorities believed there was still a “1% risk” that he might return to politics in the future.

“To avoid this, they wanted me to face corruption charges and admit guilt,” Garibashvili writes.

According to him, this demand became a “red line” that forced him to take the “most difficult step of my life” — to turn against the authorities.

“I have no other choice. I am forced to start fighting,” the former prime minister said.

On 17 August 2026, Garibashvili made his first public statement from prison. In a Facebook post, he said he had received an ultimatum in a letter sent on the instructions of Bidzina Ivanishvili. He added that he had “no other choice” but to stand against what he described as “evil that insults my dignity”.

“I tried to do everything possible to avoid taking this step, but unfortunately I have no other choice but to confront this evil that insults my dignity. I must confront this ruthless cruelty, oppression and injustice, as well as the dirty plan to destroy me and my family,” Garibashvili wrote.

He also said that Bidzina Ivanishvili and the government bear responsibility for the safety of both himself and his family.

In the letter, Garibashvili says he had remained publicly silent and patiently endured what was happening until now. However, he says the current situation has left him no choice but to begin fighting.

Letter from Georgia’s former prime minister from prison

World.title: Fair Work warning as court action looms over berry pickers' pay
World.content:
Australia's Fair Work Ombudsman has issued a stark warning to labour-hire firms and farms that are underpaying workers in the Coffs Harbour region: "We are coming for you."

The message came as Fair Work filed a case in the Federal Court against a labour-hire company accused of underpaying two workers about $20,000.

Fair Work Ombudsman Anna Booth said court action had been taken against three labour-hire companies so far this year, two of which were operating on the Coffs Coast.

"If you are underpaying workers in the Coffs Harbour region … then you should be on notice and checking your own supply chain to make sure it is compliant with the Fair Work Act," she said.

" Because we are coming for you. "

Fair Work has alleged Four Seasons Workforce Pty Ltd was paying workers on a piecework basis, according to how much they picked.

It has accused the company of not complying with the Pieceworker Guaranteed Minimum Rate, which guarantees workers are paid no less than the minimum hourly rate for casual fruit pickers under the Horticulture Industry Award 2020.

Anna Booth says court action has been filed against three companies so far this year. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Earlier this month, a report into modern slavery raised serious concerns about labour-hire firms operating on the Coffs and Mid North coasts, with some workers reporting they were earning less than $7 an hour and were living in overcrowded, squalid accommodation.

The ombudsman took action against Four Seasons Workforce, and the company's sole director, Pik Yok Chey, after Fair Work received complaints from two workers, a Chinese national and a Japanese national.

The pair were both in Australia on working holiday visas, and were both allegedly underpaid at different intervals between July 2023 and October 2024.

Four Seasons Workforce Pty Ltd could face penalties of up to $99,000 per offence and Ms Chey could face penalties of up to $19,800 per offence if the allegations are proven in the Federal Court.

The Fair Work Ombudsman has alleged the company also failed to act on compliance notices within the required time frame.

Ms Booth said Fair Work was seeing underpayments across the horticultural industry.

"We see them in the labour-hire industry predominantly," she said.

"Many growers engage labour-hire companies to supply labour and … this region [Coffs Harbour] is one of our top trouble spot regions that we have identified through our investigations."

Kun Du was working on a blueberry farm in the Coffs Harbour region from June and October 2024. ( Supplied: Fair Work Ombudsman)

'I had to borrow money'

When Chinese national Kun Du was working on a blueberry farm on the Coffs Coast, she was allegedly paid so little that she could not afford groceries.

"At times, I had to borrow money from the supervisor on site," Ms Du said in a statement provided by Fair Work.

When she took her case to Fair Work, Four Seasons Workforce allegedly paid her $5,000.

In a statement, Fair Work said the company also allegedly repaid $14,065 to a Japanese national after the ombudsman started legal action.

"When I saw the money, it felt like justice had been served," Ms Du said.

The Fair Work Ombudsman is taking a labour-hire company to court after it allegedly underpaid workers. (ABC Landline)

Ms Booth said workers who were on temporary visas were "particularly vulnerable".

"They are often unaware of Australian terms and conditions, they're sometimes nervous about coming to the regulator," she said.

"We do want visa holders to know they have the same rights as any Australian worker, that they can obtain our support and their visa will be protected."

The ABC was unable to contact Four Seasons Workforce for a response.

The case is set to be mentioned in the Federal Court on October 20.

World.title: Gold Coast council takes housing affordability ruling to High Court, warning of statewide impacts
World.content:
Gold Coast City Council has applied to the High Court for permission to appeal against a ruling that found luxury apartments do not improve housing affordability.

The Queensland Court of Appeal ruled in July that council could not justify its approval of a luxury beach-side tower well above the area's height limit, on the basis that it would improve "housing choice and affordability".

In documents lodged with the High Court this week, the council argued the Court of Appeal's ruling "will cause significant disruption to existing approvals" not only on the Gold Coast, but across Queensland.

"It would not be economically sensible or efficient to provide affordable housing in a beachfront development because the price of any dwelling in that location would not meet the definition of affordable housing," council's submission to the High Court stated.

Gold Coast City Council has been contacted for comment.

Luxury gets 'affordability' exemption

Under council's planning scheme, developers can build up to 50 per cent above an area's height limit if a project meets certain criteria ranging from improved amenity to benefits for "housing choice and affordability".

In 2023, developer Cielo Property Group applied to build a luxury high-rise in Bilinga, 10-metres above the suburb's height-limit.

Court documents show the 34-metre high development was also 121 per cent above the area's prescribed density limit.

The site of the luxury high-rise at 90-92 Pacific Parade, Bilinga, challenged in court. (ABC Gold Coast: Dominic Cansdale)

Council approved the development partly on the basis that it would benefit "housing choice and affordability".

Nearby residents appealed against the approval in the Planning and Environment Court but lost.

The Planning and Environment Court noted that, while the "very expensive apartments" would not provide affordable housing for low-to-middle income earners, it would "contribute to housing affordability through the provision of additional housing stock", helping to "alleviate pressures on supply".

But in its judgment last month, the Court of Appeal found luxury apartments designed for the "more affluent market" could not be considered a benefit to housing affordability.

"To do so would be a distortion of the ordinary meaning of affordability," Justice Shane Doyle stated.

Affordable vs affordability

Under state planning policies, "affordable housing" is defined as housing where low-to-middle-income households spend no more than 30 per cent of their income on housing costs.

But council's planning scheme, which operates under those policies, does not directly define "housing choice and affordability".

In its High Court submission, council argued the Court of Appeal interpreted "housing choice and affordability" too narrowly by equating it with "affordable housing".

There's been some community opposition to higher-density developments on the southern Gold Coast. (ABC Gold Coast: Dominic Cansdale)

Council instead argued "housing choice affordability" could also be achieved through "a mix of dwelling type, size and location in residential developments" across the entire city.

Council's submission also asserted that building affordable housing on prime beachfront land worth "tens of millions of dollars" would not be economically practical or reasonable.

It is not clear when the High Court will decide on whether to accept council's application to appeal.

Gold Coast councillors will be briefed on the legal action at next Tuesday's full council meeting.

World.title: Jarrod Bleijie refuses review into Olympics contractor with alleged bikie links
World.content:
Queensland's deputy premier is refusing to review the contract of an Olympics developer, which has been subject to allegations of links to bikie gangs in an inquiry this week.

It comes after the administrator of the Construction, Forestry and Maritime Employees Union (CFMEU) issued a scathing statement, calling the alleged conduct "morally repugnant".

Inquiry into Queensland's CFMEU branch Queensland's CFMEU inquiry has heard three Melbourne men linked to the Comancheros bikie gang flew to Brisbane before one allegedly threatened a construction worker at a major government project.

BMD came under scrutiny in the CFMEU commission of inquiry this week, amid allegations it hired a security company linked to the Comancheros outlaw motorcycle gang in 2024.

The state government appointed the "Queensland-born and bred" company to undertake early works at Victoria Park in July this year, the site of the new Brisbane stadium for the 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games.

Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie said he was not aware of the allegations made in the inquiry when BMD was awarded the Olympics contract.

"I didn't award the contract, GIICA (Games Independent Infrastructure and Coordination Authority) awarded the contract after an independent procurement process," Mr Bleijie said.

BMD said it wouldn’t comment further on matters while the inquiry was ongoing.

The Queensland government appointed BMD to undertake early works in Victoria Park in July. (ABC News: Chris Gillette)

Donation deflection

BMD has donated more than $22,000 to the Queensland LNP this year.

Mr Bleijie was asked, given the allegations, whether the party should consider returning the funds.

"Have you asked the Labor Party are they going to return all the CFMEU donations they received over 10 years?" he said.

A BMD spokesperson said, "all relevant disclosures are made in accordance with applicable electoral laws and are publicly available through the relevant electoral disclosure registers".

Labor has consistently maintained it will not run a public commentary on the inquiry, amid untested allegations made against its former ministers.

Mr Bleijie was quizzed, given this week's allegations, if he would refrain from making public statements on what was heard.

" Absolutely not. I'm going to run a public commentary every single bloody day of the commission of inquiry, because people need the truth exposed, and that's why we set the royal commission up. "

'Morally repugnant'

The inquiry heard this week allegations a trio of bikies made death threats against a worker at Brisbane's Centenary Bridge site in 2024.

It was alleged the men, who flew up from Melbourne, were picked up by an employee of the security company BMD had hired for the development.

The CFMEU inquiry heard bikie gangs travelled to Queensland to allegedly threaten construction site workers. (ABC News: Brigham Edgar)

The inquiry heard one of them told the crane operator, "I'll f***en burn your house down c*** and kill your kids brother … I f***en know where you live brother".

In a statement, CFMEU Administrator Michael Crosby said the behaviour was "morally repugnant and must be condemned by all".

He noted BMD was the only company to have been awarded a contract for the Olympics.

"The administration is tasked with removing all unlawful activity or use of violence.

"We expect the employers to be held to the same level of account."

Mr Bleijie said he was not condoning any of the behaviour but put little stock in the statement.

World.title: UK YouTuber Yung Filly facing retrial on allegations he raped young fan
World.content:
UK YouTuber and rapper Yung Filly will face a retrial on three counts of rape, after being acquitted three weeks ago of raping a young woman after a nightclub performance in Perth.

After a trial spanning eight days, a jury found the entertainer, whose real name is Andres Barrientos, guilty of two counts of assaulting the woman in 2024.

The 30-year-old was found not guilty of two other charges of assault, and three counts of sexual penetration without consent.

But the jury could not reach verdicts on three further charges of sexual penetration, and it is those charges the prosecution is seeking to proceed to a retrial.

Yung Filly was found not guilty of rape charges after an eight day trial in July. (ABC News: David Weber)

In court on Friday, prosecutor Danielle Clarke said the complainant was "more than willing to give evidence" in a retrial.

The alleged victim, who was 20 at the time, told the court during last month's trial she had consensual sex with Mr Barrientos after the club night at Bar 120 in Hillarys.

But she said the encounter at a hotel in Perth's CBD became non-consensual when the rapper did things to her she did not want to do.

Mr Barrientos testified he did not hit the woman or hold her by the throat, and while admitting to giving her "love bites", he believed the sexual acts were all consensual.

There was no discussion on whether the retrial would be before a judge or jury.

Yung Filly is currently on bail. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor )

Mr Barrientos, who is on bail, will appear in court again next week.

He had nothing to say to media as he left the court building.

Sentencing on the two assault convictions would happen after the retrial, the court heard.

World.title: Child treated for tuberculosis attended Tasmanian daycare centre
World.content:
A childcare centre in Tasmania's north has confirmed a child who has been treated for the infectious bacterial disease tuberculosis attended the centre.

The child, whose age and gender have not been disclosed for confidentiality reasons, last attended the Kings Meadow Goodstart Early Learning Centre in mid-July.

The centre caters for children aged between six months and six years old.

A spokesperson from Goodstart said the centre was first informed of the case last week and began contacting families of children at the centre yesterday.

Close contacts of the child, including children and staff, have been offered precautionary testing, which is being coordinated by Tasmania's Department of Health and the Launceston General Hospital.

The ABC understands the risk of transmission is low and this is an isolated case.

"The centre remains open and continues to operate as normal with the rigorous hygiene and cleaning part of our usual routine," the spokesperson said.

The centre continues to operate as normal with "rigorous hygiene and cleaning part of our usual routine", the operator says. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

Tuberculosis is relatively rare in Australia, and while it can be deadly if left untreated, it can be treated with antibiotics.

The Australian Centre for Disease Control says tuberculosis causes an estimated 1.3 million deaths worldwide annually.

Countries with a high prevalence of TB include India, Indonesia, Philippines, Pakistan and Vietnam, according to the World Health Organization.

The spokesperson from Goodstart said their response had been coordinated with state authorities in alignment with their own policies.

"We've closely followed the directions of Public Health Tasmania and our own infectious diseases policy since being contacted last week," they said.

" Families with concerns are being asked to directly contact their GP or the Public Health Hotline on 1800 671 738. "

The spokesperson also said the child had attended another childcare centre in the area.

Tasmania's Department of Health lists suspected tuberculosis as an urgent category 1 medical condition requiring urgent assessment.

The Australian Centre for Disease Control website states that tuberculosis vaccinations are only recommended for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children aged under five, some healthcare workers and children born to parents from countries with high tuberculosis incidence or those travelling to countries with high instances of the disease.

The Tasmanian Health Department has been contacted for comment.

World.title: Man charged with foreign interference had 'military-style training' in Russia
World.content:
A Russian Australian man allegedly travelled to Ukraine to collect information about Ukrainian operations, with the intention to cipher that information back to Russia.

The Australian Federal Police (AFP) have revealed the allegations after charging a dual citizen with foreign interference overnight.

The 27-year-old was arrested yesterday in Sumner, in Brisbane's west, but the AFP said he was a "Victorian resident".

He has been charged with attempting to engage in intentional foreign interference and will appear in the Brisbane Magistrates Court today.

AFP Commissioner Krissy Barrett said investigators would allege that the man travelled to Russia in October 2024, where he undertook military-style training before returning to Australia.

The AFP alleges that the man travelled to Ukraine in May 2025, where he joined Ukrainian Armed Forces to gain access to information relating to their military personnel, units and locations.

He then allegedly attempted to provide the information to individuals he believed were acting on behalf of Russian intelligence.

Commissioner Barrett said there was nothing to suggest there was any threat to Australia.

The foreign interference charge carries a maximum penalty of 20 years in jail.

Alleged Russian spies charged with new offence Crown prosecutors presented a new bench charge for the couple of conspiracy to commit espionage.

It is not the first time that police have accused Russia of orchestrating foreign interference in Australia.

Australia has been one of Ukraine's most prominent supporters after Russia's invasion and has funnelled about $1.8 billion to the country in military, economic and humanitarian support over the past four years.

That seems to have coincided with a campaign of Russian espionage in Australia.

In 2024, two Russian-born Australian citizens, married couple Kira and Igor Korolev, were arrested and accused of allegedly attempting to gather and send state secrets to Russia.

Russian hackers warning The hackers are targeting systems in defence, energy and communication sectors.

In June, the charges against them were upgraded to conspiracy to commit espionage.

ASIO director Mike Burgess said his agency had forced out a "hive of spies" from an unnamed country in 2022. They were said to be trying to covertly recruit Australians and steal sensitive information.

Multiple media outlets later reported that Russia was the country running that network, although ASIO has never publicly confirmed this.

Last month, the Australian Signals Directorate (ASD) and nearly two dozen partner agencies issued a joint warning accusing Russian-linked hackers of targeting critical Australian industries, including defence, communications, energy and financial services.

In 2018, the Turnbull government announced it was expelling two Russian diplomats, who it said were undeclared intelligence operatives, as part of global action against Moscow over an alleged nerve agent attack on a former Russian spy living in the UK.

This year, authorities also charged three Chinese nationals with trying to gather intelligence on a Canberra Buddhist group for Chinese security agencies.

World.title: Hong Kong Tiananmen vigil organisers convicted
World.content:
Two former organisers of Hong Kong's decades-old vigil in remembrance of the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown have been convicted of incitement to subversion.

The decision was handed down on Friday, local time, in a national security case brought under a China-imposed law that has effectively crushed the city's previously thriving pro-democracy movement.

Lee Cheuk-yan and Chow Hang-tung, former leaders of the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China, were charged in 2021 with inciting subversion under the national security law.

Tiananmen Square candlelight vigil trial Lee Cheuk-yan and Chow Hang-tung face up to 10 years in jail if convicted of "incitement to subversion". Advocates say the trial is part of a crackdown by Beijing on long-enjoyed freedoms in Hong Kong.

They both pleaded not guilty and now face a maximum prison term of 10 years. The alliance was also found guilty.

For three decades, the city's candlelight vigil, organised by the alliance, was the only large-scale public commemoration in China of the Tiananmen Square massacre and regularly drew tens of thousands of people annually to mourn the victims.

The event was banned in 2020 during the first year of the COVID-19 pandemic, weeks before Beijing imposed its security law on Hong Kong to quell the 2019 massive anti-government protests.

Observers said their trial symbolises the erosion of freedom of expression in the former British colony, which returned to Chinese rule in 1997.

They are expected to be sentenced at a later date.

Organisers accused of inciting the overthrow of China's ruling party

During the trial, prosecutors said the case was not political and focused on what they viewed as a call by the alliance to incite others to overthrow the leadership of China's ruling Communist Party through unlawful means, pointing to "ending one-party rule", one of the group's core demands.

But Lee told the court that the call was not about ending the party's leadership but about moving toward democracy, letting the people decide who leads them, and that the Communist Party should not enforce "dictatorship".

Tens of thousands of people at a candlelight vigil at Hong Kong's Victoria Park on June 4, 2014, to mark the 25th anniversary of the Tiananmen Square massacre. (Reuters/Bobby Yip)

Chow, a barrister who defended herself, said "ending one-party rule" meant ending a state where power was unrestricted. She criticised how the standard for determining right and wrong was turned upside down in this case.

In a Patreon post on Thursday, she recalled being shackled in handcuffs, and in waist and ankle chains, for trips to court from prison, saying she was walked by correctional service officers "like a dog".

"Justice lives in the hearts of the people. There is no need to look up to this kind of top-down ruling, and one verdict doesn't matter much," she said.

The trial, initially scheduled for 75 days, moved faster than expected and concluded its closing statements on the 24th day.

When it began in January, Albert Ho, another defendant in the case, entered a guilty plea in a move that typically could result in a reduced sentence.

Lee and Chow are expected to plead for lesser penalties at a separate hearing and could be sentenced at a later date alongside Ho.

Supporters cast doubt on allegations

Dozens of people lined up outside the court under drizzling rain ahead of the hearing.

Tang Ngok-kwan, a former alliance member, said police would not let him join the line if he brought "sensitive" materials, including bookmarks printed with "vindicate June 4" — the date of the Tiananmen Square crackdown.

He decided not to go into court.

Amnesty International Hong Kong Overseas spokesperson Fernando Cheung said the verdict "underlines how Hong Kong's National Security Law is being used to punish people for peacefully remembering one of the darkest chapters in recent Chinese history".

"For decades, Hong Kong was the only place on Chinese soil where large-scale public remembrance of the Tiananmen crackdown could take place.

"Today's decision marks another grim milestone in the government's deliberate campaign to erase that legacy and silence those who seek truth, justice and accountability."

Over seven weeks in 1989, students led peaceful pro-democracy protests centred on Beijing's Tiananmen Square. (AP: Sadayuki Mikami) (AP: Sadayuki Mikami)

Hundreds of people, and possibly thousands, were killed in the 1989 crackdown as military tanks rolled into the centre of Beijing.

It was a pivotal moment in China's modern history, determining that the market reforms that transformed the country into the world's second-largest economy would not be coupled with political liberalisation.

After COVID-19 restrictions were lifted, the former vigil site in Hong Kong was occupied instead each June 4 by a carnival and market stalls organised by pro-Beijing groups.

Beijing said the 2020 security law was necessary for the city's stability.

Many leading activists have been jailed under the same law, including pro-democracy former media tycoon Jimmy Lai.

Under the drastic political changes, dozens of civil society groups also dissolved, including the alliance.

AP

World.title: 'This is a united club': Swans AFLW captain and coach speak to media
World.content:
Sydney Swans AFLW captain Lucy McEvoy has said her players have had "open conversations" in the wake of the scandal that has engulfed her club and led to five men's players being suspended for the rest of the season.

McEvoy, along with AFLW coach Colin O'Riordan, spoke to the media on Friday afternoon, saying the women's program supports the sanctions imposed on Isaac Heeney, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner, Riley Bice and James Jordon.

Live Moment Look back at how ABC readers and other Australians responded to this live moment. The press conference has ended AFLW players would like to have say in whether five suspended men's players return Lucy McEvoy is asked if the AFLW players have discussed whether they want the five suspended players to return to the club. She tells the media that conversation has not happened but, when the time comes, the AFLW players would like to be part of the discussion. 'Moment for all women to stand together', McEvoy Here is more from Lucy McEvoy, speaking about the wider issue at the heart of this week's scandal. "There's no doubt, I think, a lot of women in the community are all feeling the same. "It's obviously an issue within the community that needs to be addressed, and I think this week it has been. "I applaud the club in the way they have handled it, and respected us as a women's program. "I think it's an important moment for all women to stand together and understand that all women deserve respect." Show more

Those five players will miss the remainder of the AFL season following club-imposed suspensions for breaking team standards in Melbourne earlier this week.

Victoria Police are investigating a sexual assault allegation, where it is alleged one player touched a woman without her consent. No charges have been laid, and no-one has been formally interviewed.

Speaking on Friday, McEvoy said the AFLW program supported the club-imposed suspensions to the five men's players, and said their actions did not reflect the Swans as a club.

"On behalf of the playing group, we also support the club in the sanctions that were handed down," McEvoy said.

"To the players, we are incredibly disappointed, as a lot of people were.

"We know that the actions of those five players are not a reflection of the broader club."

McEvoy said it had been a big week for the women's program, who will face Essendon at the Sydney Cricket Ground this weekend.

The Swans were hoping to celebrate this week's double-header with the men's round 24 clash with North Melbourne following the AFLW match on Sunday afternoon.

In the wake of this week's scandal, McEvoy said members of the women's program were processing their emotions and the situation.

"We've had some really open conversations as a group this week, and with the club more broadly," she said.

"We've felt the support both internally and externally as well.

"The girls are working through their emotions as they see fit for themselves."

When asked how this week has affected the reputation of the Sydney Swans, McEvoy said the club, both men's and women's teams, must work to regain the public's trust.

"There's no doubt the club has taken a reputational hit," she said.

"We will do whatever we can as a club, both programs, to make sure we build back the trust and respect of our members and fans, and the community more broadly."

O'Riordan, who played 34 AFL matches for the Swans between 2015 and 2022 before becoming the club's AFLW coach this season, said he was disappointed that he had to address this scandal.

"The actions of a small number of people have impacted a lot of people, especially the women in our football club and wider community," he said.

"As a man who was brought up with strong morals and a strong sense of what is right and wrong, [it's] disappointing to be standing here today and be talking about something like this.

"Growing up, I was always taught you treat everyone with respect, and that respect is a fundamental pillar of how you live your life.

"That is especially important in how you treat women."

O'Riordan said the club had remained "incredibly united" in the wake of the scandal.

"This is a united club. It always has been and always will be," he said.

World.title: Dual citizen arrested in Brisbane, accused of spying on Ukrainian army for Russia
World.content:
Updated NationalQueenslandCourts Dual citizen arrested in Brisbane, accused of spying on Ukrainian army for Russia Cloe Read and Alexander Darling Updated August 21, 2026 — 2:44pm ,first published 11:35am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A Russian-Australian citizen has been arrested by federal police in Brisbane over allegations he attempted to engage in intentional foreign interference. Vladimir Teslov, a 27-year-old man from Victoria, was arrested at Sumner, in Brisbane’s south-west, on Thursday. Teslov is accused of travelling to Russia in October 2024 for military-style training, returning to Australia, and then travelling to Ukraine in May 2025 to join the Ukrainian armed forces. Loading “It is alleged he subsequently provided, or attempted to provide, information obtained in Ukraine to individuals he believed were acting on behalf of Russian intelligence services,” a statement from the AFP said.



They said elements of the offence occurred while the man was in Australia and offshore, and they would allege his conduct created a risk to the safety and security of Ukrainian military personnel. The arrest came following an investigation by the Counter Foreign Interference Task Force. AFP Commissioner Krissy Barrett said that investigation began in June. She said this was the first time a person with links to Russia had been charged with attempting to engage in foreign interference since new laws were introduced in 2018. Police said they executed search warrants on Thursday at homes at Sumner and Sinnamon Park. On Friday, they searched properties in the Brisbane suburbs of Springwood and Petrie Terrace and a person at St Lucia, and seized electronic devices that were taken for forensic examinations.



Teslov was scheduled to appear in the Brisbane Magistrates Court on Friday. Barrett also stressed there was no threat to Australia as a result of the man’s alleged offending. “There is nothing to suggest he received any military training in Australia and, in terms of the training he undertook in Russia, that is part of our ongoing investigations,” she said. “There is no risk of him working for an Australian government agency that would pose a risk to Australia.” She said further charges could be laid after officers finished examining a number of electronic devices and other items seized in the Thursday arrest.



Barrett did not go into detail about what police meant when they said the man “believed” he was providing information to Russian intelligence. She declined to say whether police had begun their investigation on the advice of Ukraine. Asked whether the man would have been charged if he was accused of supplying Ukraine with Russian information, she replied: “We target criminal offending, not countries. “Our job is ensuring that Australia does not become a safe haven for people who think they can conduct foreign interference on our shores. This is about sending a message.” Get alerts on significant breaking news as happens.

World.title: Catholic Schools NSW sacks Dallas McInerney, former police minister gives evidence
World.content:
Catholic Schools NSW has sacked its chief executive officer Dallas McInerney after his damaging appearance in the witness box at the Independent Commission Against Corruption, as the Catholic Church seeks to insulate itself from a growing donations scandal. Board members moved against McInerney on Friday morning as the corruption watchdog heard new details of an at-times comical campaign of surveillance and intimidation against the state’s police minister ordered at the behest of Sydney developer Jean Nassif. Dallas McInerney was identified as a target to help win a contract with the National Catholic Education Commission. Monique Westermann The intimidation and smear campaign, which is unrelated to McInerney but being explored under the same Operation Rosny inquiry, included false assertions that cabinet minister David Elliott was having an affair. The false claim emerged in part from surveillance undertaken by private detective Shane De Kauwe, whom the ICAC alleges was paid by Nassif. But the one-time Australian Federal Police officer made a series of errors, including monitoring a house Elliott no longer lived in.



“In hindsight, I probably should have taken more action against it,” Elliott told the ICAC. “Is it morally reprehensible for somebody to monitor a cabinet minister based on gossip and innuendo and repeat it? Yes. But you can see by the fact that he was monitoring the wrong house, I probably had very little reason to be worried.” David Elliott outside the ICAC on Friday. Peter Rae Earlier, Catholic Schools NSW released a statement confirming McInerney’s contract had been terminated following his appearance at the ICAC on over the past two weeks. The ICAC alleges McInerney potentially broke donation laws by directing hundreds of thousands of dollars towards a conservative Christian Liberal Party sub-faction known as the Reformers.



McInerney told the Herald after his sacking: “When the inquiry started, I said I would privilege the position of the company before my own. That is why I stood aside. Related Article Updated

Operation Rosny Former minister on verge of tears over sacking, realisation she was ‘used’ by a friend “I note the inquiry continues its important work, and we are months away from findings and conclusions. “I will forever remain grateful for the opportunity to serve, and hope I have made some positive contributions along the way.” Multiple people advised the school funding organisation to allow McInerney to resign, but the board decided to terminate his contract.



In a statement, Catholic Schools NSW said that the ICAC inquiry was of “deep concern” to the organisation and its stakeholders. “The board will work constructively … to ensure there is an externally conducted review of [our] operations,” the statement said. The organisation did not respond to questions about whether the review would be made public. Investigators claim up to $265,000 in schools funding was diverted to two companies, Beckington and JPG Advisory, via sham invoices. Beckington was run by Christian Ellis, a key figure behind the Reformers, as well as lobbyist and former political staffer Jeremy Greenwood. The ICAC says Beckington and JPG did little or no work for Catholic Schools NSW, and the monthly retainers and sign-on fees were instead used to prop up the work of the Reformers. The ICAC argues funding for the group between 2019 and 2023 ultimately benefited the Liberal Party and therefore constitutes a political donation. McInerney has repeatedly denied knowledge of such a scheme.



Catholic Schools NSW was formed in 2016 to replace the Catholic Education Commission after bishops at the time expressed a desire for a more “appropriate, efficient and transparent” administration. McInerney’s role as a Liberal Party powerbroker was well known to the Catholic Schools NSW board as well as the Catholic Church and Archbishop Anthony Fisher. Senior counsel for the commission Dr Peggy Dwyer. Sam Mooy McInerney was on Wednesday accused of destroying evidence that could be relevant to the ICAC’s Operation Rosny inquiry – a claim he denied. The senior counsel leading the watchdog’s case against a group of conservative Liberal Party operatives was left dumbstruck when McInerney revealed he had performed a factory reset on his iPhone and iPad over the weekend while still sworn in as a witness.



McInerney claimed he erased everything on his phone because the National Australia Bank had placed a block on his main spending account due to a suspicious overseas transaction. Elliott, the former cabinet minister, told the ICAC on Friday that the developer Nassif “went nuts” after Elliott campaigned against development in his electorate. David Elliott speaks to the media after his ICAC appearance. Peter Rae He said he was then tailed by private investigators, subjected to death threats and confronted by Nassif on two occasions. In the first approach, Elliott said Nassif confronted him at Castle Towers and demanded to speak to him about his developments. Elliott said he told Nassif he didn’t speak to property developers.



Nassif then made another approach to Elliott at a pub in Parramatta, where he told the MP he wanted to introduce him to his daughter, and again demanded to speak with Elliott about development. Elliott says he refused. Elliott said his chief of staff, Tanya Raffoul, was “threatened” by Nassif multiple times through the Lebanese community. Raffoul went to the same church as Nassif. In one instance Raffoul was called into a meeting with Nassif, who claimed to have photos of Elliott. Elliott told the ICAC Nassif said words to the effect of “you’re going to have to spill your guts on him [Elliott] and we’re going to need you to resign and essentially turn on him, and that you know his career would be ending the next day”. Elliott said he became aware there were negative stories about him being briefed to journalists while he was a government minister. He said he formed the view Nassif was behind the campaign because “he had left a message on my mobile that he was going to get me”.

World.title: An elegant, classy stay with warm Kiwi hospitality
World.content:
★★★★ Reviews & adviceHotel reviews An elegant, classy stay with warm Kiwi hospitality Sheriden Rhodes August 21, 2026 — 2:29pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The hotel The Clements Hotel, Cambridge, New Zealand Clements Hotel, Cambridge. Check-in We arrive at the newly opened Clements Hotel via a walled garden where diners quaff wine beneath sunny yellow umbrellas. Cameron Kellow, the general manager (hailing from Scotland’s grand Scone Palace), welcomes us. We’re handed a complimentary glass of Clements Royale champagne and shown to our room.



The look 



Inside one of the hotel’s Stable Suites. There are 29 rooms and suites across three floors designed in classic style with complimentary mini bars (first night only), clothes steamer and Manuka Dreams sleep mist. Contemporary attic-level rooms offer street views while restored Edwardian rooms feature soaring ceilings. Our spacious executive room offers a king-size bed and porcelain-tiled bathroom with a freestanding tub positioned invitingly beneath a skylight. Plush furniture, Frette linen and curved velvet bedheads lend a luxe feel. The Clements Suite with its coveted 30-square-metre terrace is the pick. Former century-old horse stables to the rear, meanwhile, have been converted into three interconnecting rooms offering a luxe cottage aesthetic. Food + drink The hotel breakfast. Anchoring the hotel is the Gallery Restaurant where exposed brick walls, high beamed ceiling and a wall of bi-fold doors open onto the terrace, lawn and garden. Comfy banquet seating encourages diners to linger over superb a la carte breakfasts. A basic poached egg on sourdough dish is elevated by fresh herbs and greens picked straight from the garden. While also featuring local Waikato produce, the dinner menu sadly doesn’t hit the mark (yet).



The charming corner bar spilling out onto Duke Street is popular with locals and guests alike, morphing from morning coffee and pastries to evening aperitifs. The coffee’s fine but arguably Cambridge’s best is found nearby at Daydream Espresso. The Stable Suites. Downstairs, the original 150-year-old basement is now “1866”, a speakeasy bar. The bar is currently only open three nights a week, so I miss the chance of a martini in the dimly lit space inspired by Chicago’s Prohibition-era haunts. Out + about Take a heart-pumping ride along the mighty Waikato River in a 450hp V8 jet boat traversing the narrow Cambridge gorge, punctuated by squeal-inducing 360-degree spins. Owner and guide Aaron Crossan points out gushing waterfalls, native bush, wildlife, fish and rapids (see camjet.co.nz).



Tackle all or part of the picturesque 60-kilometre Te Awa River Trail on a self-guided e-bike tour. Start with lunch at the bucolic Punnet Eatery located in a former strawberry farm, cycle through rolling farmland and native bush and skirt the riverbank on your return to the town’s velodrome (see riversideadventures.co.nz). Dine on antipasti through secondi to dolce at the much-loved trattoria Alpino, housed in a century-old post office, known for hearty pastas, wood-fire pizzas and its warm and welcoming atmosphere (alpino.co.nz). Enjoy gin, vodka and limoncello tastings at the Cambridge Distillery, located directly behind the Clements Hotel (thecambridgedistillery.co.nz). The verdict An elegant, classy stay with warm Kiwi hospitality.



Essentials Fly to Hamilton Airport, 90 minutes south of Auckland on new direct Jetstar (jetstar.com) flights four times weekly from Sydney. Cambridge is a 15-minute drive from the airport.

From $250 a night. The property has two accessible rooms. 68 Duke Street, Cambridge, New Zealand. Phone: +64 7 974 9050. See clements.co.nz Our rating out of five ★★★★ Highlight

G&T’s in the bar made from the hotel’s own gin crafted by the Cambridge Distillery Co using an 1860s Irish recipe.



Lowlight

Dinner was lacklustre, but given the hotel was newly opened we put it down to teething issues. The writer stayed as a guest of the Clements Hotel and Waikato Tourism. See waikatonz.com

World.title: Swans AFLW captain says club has taken ‘reputational hit’
World.content:
Sydney Swans AFLW captain Lucy McEvoy says the club has “taken a reputational hit” after five male players were stood down for breaching club standards and a police investigation into an alleged sexual assault continues. However, McEvoy said the actions of those players – James Jordon, Chad Warner, Isaac Heeney, Riley Bice and Nick Blakey – were not a reflection of the broader club, and called on fans to support the team at Sunday’s double-header at the SCG, which will be the second time the women’s team have played a competitive match at the historic venue. Loading “On behalf of the playing group, we also support the club in the sanctions that were handed down to the players,” McEvoy said on Friday. “We are incredibly disappointed, as a lot of people are, with what’s occurred at the beginning of this week, and we know that the actions of those five players are not a reflection of the broader club and the programs more broadly.”



The men’s captain Callum Mills spoke to the women’s team earlier in the week, but McEvoy confirmed that none of the five suspended players had been in contact with the AFLW team. McEvoy denied there was any rift between the AFL and AFLW programs, saying the club was “absolutely united”. The two programs united this week and even shared a barbecue at the club’s headquarters. McEvoy said the women’s team had not discussed how they would feel about any of the five players returning to the club in the future, but when asked if it was something she would like input in, she said, “absolutely, yes”. Swans AFLW captain Lucy McEvoy and coach Colin O’Riordan front the media. Getty Images Mills acknowledged that the women’s game at the SCG had been “overshadowed” when speaking at a press conference earlier on Friday, but asked members and fans to support the AFLW team.



“It’s a historic weekend for the football club; it’s our first double-header of AFLW and men’s program together on the SCG,” Mills said. “And whilst this has overshadowed it, I think it’s an incredible, powerful moment that we’ve come together, and we celebrate that moment of AFLW program out on the SCG.” McEvoy said the women’s team had received a huge amount of support this week from the club and community, and encouraged fans to attend the double-header, despite the scandal surrounding the club. Sydney Swans AFLW coach Colin O’Riordan and captain Lucy McEvoy on Friday. Sitthixay Ditthavong “This week was supposed to be a really big day for our football club and the W program, so to be able to get that support – and we feel it a lot, we’ve had a lot of messages through social media – and the best way that we can support us in this moment is get to the game on Sunday and hopefully break a record crowd that we once set a few years ago,” McEvoy said.



Mills went and spoke with the women’s team earlier in the week, where he “apologised for the actions of a few within our group” - which McEvoy said she was and the other women’s players appreciated. Related Article AFL off-field behaviour ‘Shocked and disappointed’: Swans captain says it’s time to hold up a mirror to his club, and society “He [Mills] was quite remorseful on behalf of the men’s program, and he’s a really class human being, Millsy,” McEvoy said. “The respect he has for us and the respect we have for him and the way he’s handled himself this week is second to none, and we couldn’t have asked more from him as a captain of the men’s program, and we really appreciate him taking the time to wrap his arms around us as a football club.” O’Riordan urged fans to help break the Swans’ AFLW home attendance record of 8264, set at their first game in 2022 at North Sydney Oval against St Kilda.



“I think for us as a club to break a record like that after such a tough week and disappointing week for the club would be incredible,” O’Riordan said. “But I think it would lift everyone and every woman in NSW and probably nationwide; it would lift them to show support, come out in your numbers and support these incredible women. I think that’s what we’re all after; I hope we can get that.”

World.title: Sucker for a pinot noir? These cheaper, lighter-bodied reds are also worth a go
World.content:
Remove items from your saved list to add more.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Fridgeable, smashable reds that are made to be enjoyed young are having their day.

Lighter-bodied reds – we’re talking pinot meunier (pinot noir’s shy cousin), gamay (the grape of Beaujolais), dolcetto, mencia, barbera, cinsault and the lighter versions of grenache – are having their day.

Fridgeable, smashable, easygoing reds that need no cellaring and are made to enjoy young. They’re cheaper than pinot noir and pair with all types of seafood, poultry and vegetable dishes.

My top three lighter-bodied reds De Bortoli The Estate Vineyard Gamay 2025, Yarra Valley ($25)

Full and very bright purple in colour; meaty, plummy and spicy on the nose, a touch of funky carbonic maceration character and bright and crisp in the mouth with lively acidity. Best’s Young Vine Pinot Meunier 2025, Great Western ($45)

Light, fresh, purple-fringed colour with a fruit-driven, grapy, raspberry aroma. The wine is light in the mouth but not too simplistic, with some forest-floor and savoury touches and fine, powdery tannins. Light and food-friendly. TarraWarra Estate Barbera 2024, Yarra Valley ($40)

Deep, bright-purple in colour and offering a fragrant nose of violets and blueberry – it has an inviting perfume, with some bunchy notes. Excellent intensity of fruit, with oak playing a merely supportive role, while tannins are refined and balanced. Can be enjoyed young but it could also benefit from keeping it a while longer.

Got a drinks question for Huon Hooke? thefullbottle@goodweekend.com.au

World.title: Suspended City of Perth CEO emailed ‘advice’ before committee meeting
World.content:
NationalWALocal council Suspended City of Perth CEO emailed ‘advice’ before committee meeting Carla Hildebrandt August 21, 2026 — 2:19pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Suspended City of Perth boss Michelle Reynolds emailed councillors just minutes before a scheduled committee meeting, offering “late advice” on a live compliance issue. The email, tabled at an Audit, Risk and Improvement Committee meeting on August 10, was sent from Reynolds’ work account at 3.49pm, just 11 minutes before the meeting was due to begin. Suspended chief executive officer Michelle Reynolds. Council voted to suspend Reynolds from her duties as chief executive officer in May, and enact an acting chief executive, after a confidential meeting was held by Local Government Inspector Tony Brown. Reynolds’ email before the meeting took issue with a report dealing with a compliance failure for 2025. It was sent to acting chief executive Maria Cooke and independent committee members Colin Murphy and Jonathan Seth. Other recipients have been blacked out on the copy released by the city.



Cooke tabled Reynolds’ email when the committee reached the compliance item, according to the meeting minutes. Related Article Updated

Local government ‘Amalgamations back on the table’, minister vows as ‘dysfunctional’ Perth council put on notice Deputy Lord Mayor David Goncalves issued a comment in the minutes, which stated Reynolds’ emailed “some, but not all, of (the committee) members, from her City of Perth email account ... offering advice, comments and suggested actions on that item”. The compliance failure Reynolds had emailed about was the only failure of 97 requirements assessed, as part of the city’s annual compliance audit return. It required her as chief executive to submit a report she completed to the committee – which she did on May 12, 2025 – and also to council, which was not done, leading to the compliance failure.



The minutes stated the reason it was not submitted to council was “not clear”, but Reynolds suggested in her email that the failure should be explained as an administrative error. “Sorry about the late advice but I have just read the ARIC papers for tonights (sic) meeting,” she wrote in the email. “...this appears to be an administrative oversight issue and should be explained as such.” In the email, Reynolds said the paper appeared to be “missing facts” and suggested a question could be put to the governance team. “If we can ensure the full explanation is available to members this would be greatly appreciated,” she wrote.



This masthead asked the City of Perth what restrictions applied to Reynolds’ communications, whether she was authorised to give advice on agenda items, and whether the email was a breach of her suspension. A City of Perth spokesperson said the matter was “confidential” and they could not comment. Local Government Inspector Tony Brown and Michelle Reynolds have been contacted for comment.

Pakistan’s former prime minister Imran Khan has been moved back to prison after spending a few hours overnight at a hospital, a spokesman for his party said on Friday.

Khan, 73, was transferred to a hospital in Islamabad early on Friday for ​a medical examination, following a Supreme Court order this week.

Former Pakistani prime minister Imran Khan. AP

A spokesperson for Khan’s party, Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf, confirmed Khan had been taken back to Adiala prison in the garrison city of Rawalpindi. Khan has been ⁠imprisoned since ​August 2023. He says the cases against ​him are politically motivated, an accusation the government denies.

His lawyers say his health has deteriorated in prison ‌and ⁠that he has lost significant vision in his right eye.

The government has said medical reports disclosed no condition requiring immediate treatment.

World.title: Women at centre of Swans saga set to sue stars and club
World.content:
SportAFLAFL off-field behaviour Women at centre of Swans saga set to sue stars and club Christine Lacy August 21, 2026 — 2:17pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Lawyers for two of the women involved in the Sydney Swans alleged sexual assault incident in a Melbourne hotel room are preparing to launch legal action in the Victorian Supreme Court against the five players and the club. The lawyer representing the two women told this masthead that the legal proceedings would be launched in the Common Law Division of the Victorian Supreme Court, with the women set to claim damages for pain and suffering, psychological injury and economic loss. The Pullman hotel in East Melbourne. Simon Schluter “We are currently investigating the circumstances and preparing to commence legal proceedings against the club and potentially the individuals involved,” Manny Carbone, a partner at Carbone Lawyers, said. “Our clients are extremely traumatised and feel that their dignity and personal rights have been seriously violated by the events of Monday.”



Five Swans players – Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, James Jordon and Riley Bice – have been suspended from play for the rest of this year for their part in the incident that unfolded in a Pullman hotel room in East Melbourne in the early hours of last Monday. A woman who visited the room has alleged she was sexually assaulted by one of the players. A police investigation is under way. Loading Star player Isaac Heeney is at the centre of the police investigation. John Karantzis, the head of personal injury law and litigation at Carbone Lawyers, described the alleged assault as “demeaning, abhorrent and simply not moral or acceptable”.



“These women were subjected to the most disgusting actions and behaviour I have ever heard about in my 28 years as a lawyer,” he told Melbourne radio station 3AW on Friday. “They’re suffering severe stress and anxiety. They’re actually fearing for their life at the moment ... they are literally in hiding and they are suffering.” The five Sydney Swans players stood down over the alleged sexual assault investigation. 9News Karantzis said there were “even a few leaders in that room” along with the five Swans players. “I can’t go into detail because this will be the subject of proceedings, criminal and civil,” Karantzis said. “However, things got out of hand. The line was crossed.”



Related Article AFL off-field behaviour ‘Shocked and disappointed’: Swans captain says it’s time to hold up a mirror to his club, and society The Sydney Swans denied there were any other Swans players or officials in the room. “The Sydney Swans can confirm that all investigations carried out by the club have consistently indicated that the only representatives of the club in the room central to the police investigation were the five players who have been stood down,” the club said in a statement on Friday morning. “We have every reason to consider that reports to the contrary are simply false. “We are respecting the process with the relevant authorities and will refrain from commencing on police matters.



“We would also like to take this opportunity to condemn some of the misinformation being reported and are now considering our legal position on those matters,” the statement read. The women’s legal action is expected to be taken via the court’s Institutional Liability List, which is a specialist personal injury list within the Common Law Division. A source close to the women involved in the incident, but not authorised to speak publicly, said at least one of the women was “traumatised” by the incident and subsequent fallout from the unfolding scandal. At least one of the women, they said, had already sought professional psychological treatment to help deal with the events.
