Elliott says he refused. Elliott said his chief of staff, Tanya Raffoul, was “threatened” by Nassif multiple times through the Lebanese community. Raffoul went to the same church as Nassif. In one instance Raffoul was called into a meeting with Nassif, who claimed to have photos of Elliott. Elliott told the ICAC Nassif said words to the effect of “you’re going to have to spill your guts on him [Elliott] and we’re going to need you to resign and essentially turn on him, and that you know his career would be ending the next day”. Elliott said he became aware there were negative stories about him being briefed to journalists while he was a government minister. He said he formed the view Nassif was behind the campaign because “he had left a message on my mobile that he was going to get me”.

World.title: An elegant, classy stay with warm Kiwi hospitality
World.content:
★★★★ Reviews & adviceHotel reviews An elegant, classy stay with warm Kiwi hospitality Sheriden Rhodes August 21, 2026 — 2:29pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The hotel The Clements Hotel, Cambridge, New Zealand Clements Hotel, Cambridge. Check-in We arrive at the newly opened Clements Hotel via a walled garden where diners quaff wine beneath sunny yellow umbrellas. Cameron Kellow, the general manager (hailing from Scotland’s grand Scone Palace), welcomes us. We’re handed a complimentary glass of Clements Royale champagne and shown to our room.



The look 



Inside one of the hotel’s Stable Suites. There are 29 rooms and suites across three floors designed in classic style with complimentary mini bars (first night only), clothes steamer and Manuka Dreams sleep mist. Contemporary attic-level rooms offer street views while restored Edwardian rooms feature soaring ceilings. Our spacious executive room offers a king-size bed and porcelain-tiled bathroom with a freestanding tub positioned invitingly beneath a skylight. Plush furniture, Frette linen and curved velvet bedheads lend a luxe feel. The Clements Suite with its coveted 30-square-metre terrace is the pick. Former century-old horse stables to the rear, meanwhile, have been converted into three interconnecting rooms offering a luxe cottage aesthetic. Food + drink The hotel breakfast. Anchoring the hotel is the Gallery Restaurant where exposed brick walls, high beamed ceiling and a wall of bi-fold doors open onto the terrace, lawn and garden. Comfy banquet seating encourages diners to linger over superb a la carte breakfasts. A basic poached egg on sourdough dish is elevated by fresh herbs and greens picked straight from the garden. While also featuring local Waikato produce, the dinner menu sadly doesn’t hit the mark (yet).



The charming corner bar spilling out onto Duke Street is popular with locals and guests alike, morphing from morning coffee and pastries to evening aperitifs. The coffee’s fine but arguably Cambridge’s best is found nearby at Daydream Espresso. The Stable Suites. Downstairs, the original 150-year-old basement is now “1866”, a speakeasy bar. The bar is currently only open three nights a week, so I miss the chance of a martini in the dimly lit space inspired by Chicago’s Prohibition-era haunts. Out + about Take a heart-pumping ride along the mighty Waikato River in a 450hp V8 jet boat traversing the narrow Cambridge gorge, punctuated by squeal-inducing 360-degree spins. Owner and guide Aaron Crossan points out gushing waterfalls, native bush, wildlife, fish and rapids (see camjet.co.nz).



Tackle all or part of the picturesque 60-kilometre Te Awa River Trail on a self-guided e-bike tour. Start with lunch at the bucolic Punnet Eatery located in a former strawberry farm, cycle through rolling farmland and native bush and skirt the riverbank on your return to the town’s velodrome (see riversideadventures.co.nz). Dine on antipasti through secondi to dolce at the much-loved trattoria Alpino, housed in a century-old post office, known for hearty pastas, wood-fire pizzas and its warm and welcoming atmosphere (alpino.co.nz). Enjoy gin, vodka and limoncello tastings at the Cambridge Distillery, located directly behind the Clements Hotel (thecambridgedistillery.co.nz). The verdict An elegant, classy stay with warm Kiwi hospitality.



Essentials Fly to Hamilton Airport, 90 minutes south of Auckland on new direct Jetstar (jetstar.com) flights four times weekly from Sydney. Cambridge is a 15-minute drive from the airport.

From $250 a night. The property has two accessible rooms. 68 Duke Street, Cambridge, New Zealand. Phone: +64 7 974 9050. See clements.co.nz Our rating out of five ★★★★ Highlight

G&T’s in the bar made from the hotel’s own gin crafted by the Cambridge Distillery Co using an 1860s Irish recipe.



Lowlight

Dinner was lacklustre, but given the hotel was newly opened we put it down to teething issues. The writer stayed as a guest of the Clements Hotel and Waikato Tourism. See waikatonz.com

World.title: Swans AFLW captain says club has taken ‘reputational hit’
World.content:
Sydney Swans AFLW captain Lucy McEvoy says the club has “taken a reputational hit” after five male players were stood down for breaching club standards and a police investigation into an alleged sexual assault continues. However, McEvoy said the actions of those players – James Jordon, Chad Warner, Isaac Heeney, Riley Bice and Nick Blakey – were not a reflection of the broader club, and called on fans to support the team at Sunday’s double-header at the SCG, which will be the second time the women’s team have played a competitive match at the historic venue. Loading “On behalf of the playing group, we also support the club in the sanctions that were handed down to the players,” McEvoy said on Friday. “We are incredibly disappointed, as a lot of people are, with what’s occurred at the beginning of this week, and we know that the actions of those five players are not a reflection of the broader club and the programs more broadly.”



The men’s captain Callum Mills spoke to the women’s team earlier in the week, but McEvoy confirmed that none of the five suspended players had been in contact with the AFLW team. McEvoy denied there was any rift between the AFL and AFLW programs, saying the club was “absolutely united”. The two programs united this week and even shared a barbecue at the club’s headquarters. McEvoy said the women’s team had not discussed how they would feel about any of the five players returning to the club in the future, but when asked if it was something she would like input in, she said, “absolutely, yes”. Swans AFLW captain Lucy McEvoy and coach Colin O’Riordan front the media. Getty Images Mills acknowledged that the women’s game at the SCG had been “overshadowed” when speaking at a press conference earlier on Friday, but asked members and fans to support the AFLW team.



“It’s a historic weekend for the football club; it’s our first double-header of AFLW and men’s program together on the SCG,” Mills said. “And whilst this has overshadowed it, I think it’s an incredible, powerful moment that we’ve come together, and we celebrate that moment of AFLW program out on the SCG.” McEvoy said the women’s team had received a huge amount of support this week from the club and community, and encouraged fans to attend the double-header, despite the scandal surrounding the club. Sydney Swans AFLW coach Colin O’Riordan and captain Lucy McEvoy on Friday. Sitthixay Ditthavong “This week was supposed to be a really big day for our football club and the W program, so to be able to get that support – and we feel it a lot, we’ve had a lot of messages through social media – and the best way that we can support us in this moment is get to the game on Sunday and hopefully break a record crowd that we once set a few years ago,” McEvoy said.



Mills went and spoke with the women’s team earlier in the week, where he “apologised for the actions of a few within our group” - which McEvoy said she was and the other women’s players appreciated. Related Article AFL off-field behaviour ‘Shocked and disappointed’: Swans captain says it’s time to hold up a mirror to his club, and society “He [Mills] was quite remorseful on behalf of the men’s program, and he’s a really class human being, Millsy,” McEvoy said. “The respect he has for us and the respect we have for him and the way he’s handled himself this week is second to none, and we couldn’t have asked more from him as a captain of the men’s program, and we really appreciate him taking the time to wrap his arms around us as a football club.” O’Riordan urged fans to help break the Swans’ AFLW home attendance record of 8264, set at their first game in 2022 at North Sydney Oval against St Kilda.



“I think for us as a club to break a record like that after such a tough week and disappointing week for the club would be incredible,” O’Riordan said. “But I think it would lift everyone and every woman in NSW and probably nationwide; it would lift them to show support, come out in your numbers and support these incredible women. I think that’s what we’re all after; I hope we can get that.”

World.title: Sucker for a pinot noir? These cheaper, lighter-bodied reds are also worth a go
World.content:
Remove items from your saved list to add more.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Fridgeable, smashable reds that are made to be enjoyed young are having their day.

Lighter-bodied reds – we’re talking pinot meunier (pinot noir’s shy cousin), gamay (the grape of Beaujolais), dolcetto, mencia, barbera, cinsault and the lighter versions of grenache – are having their day.

Fridgeable, smashable, easygoing reds that need no cellaring and are made to enjoy young. They’re cheaper than pinot noir and pair with all types of seafood, poultry and vegetable dishes.

My top three lighter-bodied reds De Bortoli The Estate Vineyard Gamay 2025, Yarra Valley ($25)

Full and very bright purple in colour; meaty, plummy and spicy on the nose, a touch of funky carbonic maceration character and bright and crisp in the mouth with lively acidity. Best’s Young Vine Pinot Meunier 2025, Great Western ($45)

Light, fresh, purple-fringed colour with a fruit-driven, grapy, raspberry aroma. The wine is light in the mouth but not too simplistic, with some forest-floor and savoury touches and fine, powdery tannins. Light and food-friendly. TarraWarra Estate Barbera 2024, Yarra Valley ($40)

Deep, bright-purple in colour and offering a fragrant nose of violets and blueberry – it has an inviting perfume, with some bunchy notes. Excellent intensity of fruit, with oak playing a merely supportive role, while tannins are refined and balanced. Can be enjoyed young but it could also benefit from keeping it a while longer.

World.title: Suspended City of Perth CEO emailed ‘advice’ before committee meeting
World.content:
NationalWALocal council Suspended City of Perth CEO emailed ‘advice’ before committee meeting Carla Hildebrandt August 21, 2026 — 2:19pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Suspended City of Perth boss Michelle Reynolds emailed councillors just minutes before a scheduled committee meeting, offering “late advice” on a live compliance issue. The email, tabled at an Audit, Risk and Improvement Committee meeting on August 10, was sent from Reynolds’ work account at 3.49pm, just 11 minutes before the meeting was due to begin. Suspended chief executive officer Michelle Reynolds. Council voted to suspend Reynolds from her duties as chief executive officer in May, and enact an acting chief executive, after a confidential meeting was held by Local Government Inspector Tony Brown. Reynolds’ email before the meeting took issue with a report dealing with a compliance failure for 2025. It was sent to acting chief executive Maria Cooke and independent committee members Colin Murphy and Jonathan Seth. Other recipients have been blacked out on the copy released by the city.



Cooke tabled Reynolds’ email when the committee reached the compliance item, according to the meeting minutes. Related Article Updated

Local government ‘Amalgamations back on the table’, minister vows as ‘dysfunctional’ Perth council put on notice Deputy Lord Mayor David Goncalves issued a comment in the minutes, which stated Reynolds’ emailed “some, but not all, of (the committee) members, from her City of Perth email account ... offering advice, comments and suggested actions on that item”. The compliance failure Reynolds had emailed about was the only failure of 97 requirements assessed, as part of the city’s annual compliance audit return. It required her as chief executive to submit a report she completed to the committee – which she did on May 12, 2025 – and also to council, which was not done, leading to the compliance failure.



The minutes stated the reason it was not submitted to council was “not clear”, but Reynolds suggested in her email that the failure should be explained as an administrative error. “Sorry about the late advice but I have just read the ARIC papers for tonights (sic) meeting,” she wrote in the email. “...this appears to be an administrative oversight issue and should be explained as such.” In the email, Reynolds said the paper appeared to be “missing facts” and suggested a question could be put to the governance team. “If we can ensure the full explanation is available to members this would be greatly appreciated,” she wrote.



This masthead asked the City of Perth what restrictions applied to Reynolds’ communications, whether she was authorised to give advice on agenda items, and whether the email was a breach of her suspension. A City of Perth spokesperson said the matter was “confidential” and they could not comment. Local Government Inspector Tony Brown and Michelle Reynolds have been contacted for comment.

World.title: Women at centre of Swans saga set to sue stars and club
World.content:
SportAFLAFL off-field behaviour Women at centre of Swans saga set to sue stars and club Christine Lacy August 21, 2026 — 2:17pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Lawyers for two of the women involved in the Sydney Swans alleged sexual assault incident in a Melbourne hotel room are preparing to launch legal action in the Victorian Supreme Court against the five players and the club. The lawyer representing the two women told this masthead that the legal proceedings would be launched in the Common Law Division of the Victorian Supreme Court, with the women set to claim damages for pain and suffering, psychological injury and economic loss. The Pullman hotel in East Melbourne. Simon Schluter “We are currently investigating the circumstances and preparing to commence legal proceedings against the club and potentially the individuals involved,” Manny Carbone, a partner at Carbone Lawyers, said. “Our clients are extremely traumatised and feel that their dignity and personal rights have been seriously violated by the events of Monday.”



Five Swans players – Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, James Jordon and Riley Bice – have been suspended from play for the rest of this year for their part in the incident that unfolded in a Pullman hotel room in East Melbourne in the early hours of last Monday. A woman who visited the room has alleged she was sexually assaulted by one of the players. A police investigation is under way. Loading Star player Isaac Heeney is at the centre of the police investigation. John Karantzis, the head of personal injury law and litigation at Carbone Lawyers, described the alleged assault as “demeaning, abhorrent and simply not moral or acceptable”.



“These women were subjected to the most disgusting actions and behaviour I have ever heard about in my 28 years as a lawyer,” he told Melbourne radio station 3AW on Friday. “They’re suffering severe stress and anxiety. They’re actually fearing for their life at the moment ... they are literally in hiding and they are suffering.” The five Sydney Swans players stood down over the alleged sexual assault investigation. 9News Karantzis said there were “even a few leaders in that room” along with the five Swans players. “I can’t go into detail because this will be the subject of proceedings, criminal and civil,” Karantzis said. “However, things got out of hand. The line was crossed.”



Related Article AFL off-field behaviour ‘Shocked and disappointed’: Swans captain says it’s time to hold up a mirror to his club, and society The Sydney Swans denied there were any other Swans players or officials in the room. “The Sydney Swans can confirm that all investigations carried out by the club have consistently indicated that the only representatives of the club in the room central to the police investigation were the five players who have been stood down,” the club said in a statement on Friday morning. “We have every reason to consider that reports to the contrary are simply false. “We are respecting the process with the relevant authorities and will refrain from commencing on police matters.



“We would also like to take this opportunity to condemn some of the misinformation being reported and are now considering our legal position on those matters,” the statement read. The women’s legal action is expected to be taken via the court’s Institutional Liability List, which is a specialist personal injury list within the Common Law Division. A source close to the women involved in the incident, but not authorised to speak publicly, said at least one of the women was “traumatised” by the incident and subsequent fallout from the unfolding scandal. At least one of the women, they said, had already sought professional psychological treatment to help deal with the events.

World.title: Lawyer convicted of assault on his 12-year-old son which left him hospitalised
World.content:
A lawyer has been convicted and granted name suppression following a serious assault on his son that required him being hospitalised.

The lawyer, aged in his 50s, appeared in the Timaru District Court on Friday before Judge Campbell Savage where he was sentenced to supervision after pleading guilty to a charge of assault on a child.

The judge said the case, which began in 2022, had moved at "glacial pace".

"One's led to the inescapable conclusion that you've done just about everything in your powers to frustrate the process, including avoiding the service of summons. It seems that you've used your knowledge of the system to duck and dive attempts to get it set down, and then you've counterpunched with a flurry of meritless pre-trial applications."

Court documents obtained by RNZ detail the offending which occurred in April 2022.

The summary of facts said the lawyer and his son were boxing on a concrete area at the rear of their address.

The lawyer was a "fully grown man and the victim is a small built, 38kg 12-year-old child," the summary said.

Both were wearing boxing gloves.

The lawyer struck the victim's head causing him to bleed.

"The victim said 'please stop. I am serious'.

"The defendant then struck the victim in the face followed by the stomach. This caused the victim to cry. He went to the ground.

"The defendant continued to punch the victim on the ground. Eventually the victim said he could not breath and the defendant stopped. The victim then jumped the fence to get away."

The victim was taken to hospital and was initially diagnosed with a suspected fractured cheekbone and perforated liver, however after scans this was not the case.

He sustained extensive bruising to his head and ears and a cut above his eye.

He was admitted to hospital for three nights to allow observation and investigation of his possible injuries.

The lawyer declined to comment to police.

At sentencing the man's lawyer, Michael Sandom told the court the lawyer appeared before the court as a defendant and as a practicing lawyer.

The lawyer was convicted at Timaru District Court. (File photo) RNZ / Nate McKinnon

Sandom said he was appearing among many of his colleagues and peers, which brought a level of "embarrassment and shame".

"[He] is not a perfect person, but none of us are.

"He knows the mistake that he made, he is remorseful for what occurred and in my submission shame for what occurred is an important theme for this sentencing."

Sandom said the offending would stay with the lawyer "for the rest of his life".

The offending was "distressing and repugnant" to the lawyer.

"He's ashamed for what occurred. He can barely face it, can barely talk about it, can barely engage with it at all."

Sandom said the lawyer was a "kind and generous person" as well as an "advocate" in the criminal jurisdiction.

He accepted it was "serious" offending.

Crown prosecutor Andrew McRae said the Crown opposed the lawyer's application for a discharge without conviction and said his affidavit for name suppression did not meet the threshold.

Crown prosecutor Andrew McRae. (File photo) Stuff / Pool / Alden Williams

Judge Savage said the matter had passed through the court system "at glacial pace", with the first hearing in April 2022.

The lawyer pleaded guilty during a trial after the victim had given evidence. Judge Savage said the lawyer's claim he did not see his son's statement until trial was "implausible".

"One's led to the inescapable conclusion that you've done just about everything in your powers to frustrate the process, including avoiding the service of summons. It seems that you've used your knowledge of the system to duck and dive attempts to get it set down, and then you've counterpunched with a flurry of meritless pre-trial applications."

Judge Savage said it was "charitable" to say the lawyer's guilty plea came at the 11th hour.

"It came as the clock was striking 12."

He said he had no doubt the lawyer loved his son "with all your heart".

In terms of aggravating factors, the judge pointed to the victim's age and the breach of trust.

Judge Savage declined to discharge the lawyer without a conviction, but did grant final name suppression.

He said he did not see the lawyer as a risk of re-offending.

The lawyer has been practicing for more than a decade. The New Zealand Law Society register does not say whether he holds a practicing certificate.

RNZ asked the New Zealand Law Society how the lawyer was able to continue practicing while the matter was before the court.

A spokesperson said the Law Society took any concerns regarding criminal offending by lawyers "seriously".

"Personal conduct by a lawyer may be considered under the complaints and disciplinary framework in the Lawyers and Conveyancers Act 2006 (the Act) in certain circumstances.

"However, a lawyer who holds a current practising certificate and admits to, or is found guilty of, criminal offending is not automatically suspended from practice."

The spokesperson said concerns or complaints must first be considered by independent Standards Committees who may refer matters to the New Zealand Lawyers and Conveyancers Disciplinary Tribunal, if the conduct was "sufficiently serious".

"In addition, section 40 of the Act provides that a lawyer who has applied to renew their practising certificate may continue to practise while the application is being considered. This may include cases where proceedings are ongoing."

Asked if a lawyer could be suspended pending a complaint, the spokesperson said only the tribunal could make an order that a lawyer be suspended from practice, including for an interim period while any disciplinary process is underway, or strike a lawyer off the roll of barristers and solicitors following referral from a Standards Committee.

The Disciplinary Tribunal is administered by the Ministry of Justice.

Asked why the register did not have the expiry date for the lawyer's practising certificate, the spokesperson said the Society was unable to comment on individual cases for privacy reasons.

"Speaking generally, practising certificates have an expiry date of 30 June each year."

Ministry of Justice acting group manager of National Service Delivery Louisa Carroll said the Ministry could not comment on the circumstances of any individual lawyer or active court proceedings.

Asked about the lawyer receiving legal aid clients, Carroll said legal aid providers must meet and maintain approval requirements and comply with the Legal Services Act, their legal aid provider contract, and professional obligations.

"Legal aid providers are also required to notify the Ministry within five working days if they are charged with, or convicted of, an offence punishable by imprisonment."

"Where the Ministry becomes aware of concerns about a provider, it may consider those concerns through its complaints, audit, quality assurance and provider approval processes."

Carroll said depending on the circumstances, the Ministry may take a range of actions, including imposing restrictions on a provider, modifying or cancelling their approval to undertake legal aid work, or referring matters to the New Zealand Law Society.

"Approved providers remain eligible to receive legal aid assignments unless their approval is changed, restricted, suspended, or cancelled.

World.title: Shane Jones talks up $50m-$100m koi carp policy amid Treaty stoush over Waikato rivers
World.content:
The government is undermining a Treaty settlement and the health of Waikato and Waipā rivers by prioritising its political interests, Waikato-Tainui says.

The major iwi said it was "unacceptable" to pause Plan Change 1 provisions until 2032, that doing so overrides judicial decisions in favour of the government's donors, and would subject the catchment to "another six years of degradation".

But the Resources Minister Shane Jones argues the new planning system would achieve much the same outcomes, and was promising to campaign on spending $50 million to help eradicate koi carp in the area.

Federated Farmers was also hailing the pause, saying it gave farmers "much needed breathing room" while the resource management system was overhauled.

Ministers on Wednesday announced changes to the Natural Environment Bill replacing the Resource Management Act they said would make the system more practical for food and fibre production.

"The changes will remove unnecessary complexity, better reflect real-world farming and horticultural practices, and provide greater certainty for investment and day-to-day operations," RMA Reform Minister Chris Bishop said.

RMA Reform Minister Chris Bishop. (File photo) RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

That included removing resource caps from the environmental limits framework, expanding what counts as "existing use", extending permits for water infrastructure to 35 years, allowing councils to permit or consent activities already causing adverse effects on waterways (so long as those effects will be curbed over time), and shifting from a model of "no net loss" of indigenous biodiversity to "protect significant indigenous biodiversity".

As well as the previously announced removal of Mana Whakahono ā Rohe agreements, Bishop said the amendments would also include "targeted action on Plan Changes 1 and 2 to provide respective certainty for farmers and growers in the Waikato and Manawatū-Whanganui while the new planning system is put in place".

Plan Change 1 was a set of farming regulations in the Waikato council's Regional Plan designed to protect the rivers by managing nitrogen, phosphorus, sediment and bacteria across the catchments, requiring farmers and landowners to identify and manage environmental risks through Farm Environment plans and other measures.

The Plan Change stems from Te Ture Whaimana o Te Awa o Waikato - the Vision and Strategy for the Waikato River which was negotiated between iwi and the Crown out of the Waikato-Tainui Treaty settlement - and takes precedence over other regional plans and national policy statements.

The Environment Court made a ruling in June directing Waikato Regional Council to make 20 specific changes, but confirming that once those were done the plan would have been finalised.

In a statement issued as New Zealand First's Deputy Leader early last month, Resources Minister Shane Jones said Plan Change 1 "must be paused before it becomes a bureaucratic death sentence for farmers and growers across the region".

He confirmed to RNZ on Friday the RMA changes would put Plan Change 1 on hold until 2032, saying the Treaty settlement for the Waikato River was "not to be deprecated, however food security cannot play second fiddle to any Treaty settlement or any regional council planning initiative".

"Plan 1 was going to terminate veggie growing in Waikato, and New Zealand First will never acquiesce with the termination of food production in Waikato."

He indicated the pause was likely to become indefinite - effectively a scrapping of PC1.

"Sadly, Waikato Regional Council and Tainui spent too long on this Plan 1 indulgence, and now the new regime is going to supersede what may have been a good idea in the days of Helen Clark, but life has passed those days by."

However, he believed the new planning system would achieve much the same ends.

"The new RMA system has got statutory criteria that will allow for Plan 1 to achieve, in a different form, various outcomes ... I think all iwi need to accept that farmers and veggie growers-they've vastly improved their growing systems. Science and technology has significantly improved, but those types of improvements now have to be mediated through a new statutory regime."

Waikato-Tainui chairperson Tukoroirangi Morgan said the pause "puts political interests ahead of the health of the Waikato and Waipā Rivers and undermines Treaty settlement commitments".

Waikato-Tainui chairperson Tukoroirangi Morgan. (File photo) RNZ / Cole Eastham-Farrelly

"After 14 years of work by iwi, farmers and growers, councils, industry, environmental and community groups, it is extraordinary that the Government would simply press pause now, when the process has reached its conclusion," he said.

"We know this is election year, but this is bad news for people and organisations who follow the rule of law and in the next breath have the government step in to override judicial directions at the behest of their political donors."

"Our catchments will now be subject to another six years of degradation which is completely and utterly unacceptable."

Waikato Regional Council similarly said it was disappointing the government had not sought its advice or input on the decision, saying the plan change had been developed by a group including sector, industry and community interests in response to government direction and an independent audit from the Auditor-General.

"It is clear those operating lawfully can continue to do so until 2032 when the responsible authority will transition PC1 into the new planning system. It raises questions for the people who have operated unlawfully," chief executive Chris McClay said.

"PC1 has been one of the most significant and complex planning processes undertaken in the Waikato region. It represents almost $30 million of ratepayer investment and many years of scientific analysis, community engagement, hearings and legal processes.

"Water quality is one of the region's most significant environmental concerns, reflecting its importance to community wellbeing, cultural values, recreation and the region's economic resilience. Waikato Regional Council remains committed to working alongside central government, iwi, communities, farmers, growers, industry and other stakeholders to protect and improve the health and wellbeing of the Waikato and Waipā rivers."

A koi carp. (File photo) Supplied /Stella McQueen

Jones urged patience and trust.

"It seems to me at the nub of this issue is that Waikato and Tainui believe they had a deal with the regional council, and this deal they fear is not going to be fully implemented via the RMA.

"My plea to them is just trust that the new regime - which has the blessings of our Parliament - will deliver the vast majority of what they've sought to achieve for well over a decade.

"Nothing trumps the supreme lawmaking power of Parliament, and our Parliament is ushering a new RMA regime in, and that regime will create a new set of legal conditions for food production, which will void and make unnecessary plan one."

He said Bishop had advised the Cabinet that nothing the government was doing violated any Treaty of Waitangi settlement.

Federated Farmers backed the pause, saying it was a "really positive step for Waikato farmers and a direct response to the concerns we've been raising".

"We've been saying for months that it made no sense to force farmers into a new set of rules when the Government is in the middle of overhauling the RMA, freshwater rules and the farm planning system," president Chris Woolerton said.

"Those farmers were staring down a huge amount of uncertainty and compliance cost just to keep doing what they're already doing ... bringing these requirements into line with the national system is a commonsense and pragmatic approach."

Woolerton said Federated Farmers was frustrated the government had not gone further by addressing restrictions on land-use flexibility.

"This is potentially a major issue for vegetable production in the Waikato ... we need farmers to be able to respond when the market needs more vegetables, not have regulations making it harder to change land use."

NZ First to campaign on $50m to $100m for tackling koi carp - Jones

Jones was adamant part of the problem with the rivers' health was koi carp.

"The threat to the Waikato River is as much to do with the koi carp as well as veggie growers and farmers.

The Waikato River. (File photo) RNZ / Libby Kirkby-McLeod

"I've been told over many years that the koi carp is an extraordinarily dangerous and destructive pest in the water-based ecosystems of that area, but it's just never attracted enough government capital either towards the council or to the tangata whenua."

He intended to do something about it.

"The thing to also bear in mind and which I'm going to campaign on, I think we should allocate at least $50m to $100m over time - working with Tainui, working with the council - to eradicate as much as possible the main pest in that area ... the koi carp."

"This time round, New Zealand First is going to deliver that type of practical assistance."

World.title: Air New Zealand forced to BYO fuel due to contaminated batch in Fiji
World.content:
Air New Zealand is among several airlines carrying extra fuel and cancelling services as a response to fuel contamination in Fiji.

A spokesperson for the airline told RNZ that over the past two days measures had been taken to manage fuel restrictions in Fiji.

This included "tankering fuel, cancelling one service, and upgauging two services to our Widebody aircraft".

The spokesperson said affected passengers had been moved to other services departing the same day.

The airline would continue to minimise disruptions, they said.

The ABC reported both Qantas and Virgin Airlines were also forced to bring in excess fuel to make the return journey to Australia.

Virgin Australia on Thursday cancelled two services on its Fiji route, according to the ABC.

The airline confirmed planes were being forced to stop halfway at airports in New Caledonia and Vanuatu to make the journey back to Australia and Fiji.

Sources had told the ABC the contamination related to an excessive electrical charge in a batch of fuel stored at the airport.

The source indicated it could be resolved soon or escalate into a more significant issue.

The ABC also reported pilots had been told the problem may continue until the end of the month.

Fiji Airports did not confirm to the ABC the cause of the contamination issue.

A spokesperson said they were making "operational adjustments" and the airport was "closely monitoring the current aviation fuel situation".

"Nadi International Airport remains open and operational, with established safety and operational protocols being maintained," it told the ABC.

World.title: Charities call for more state support to weather 'perfect storm'
World.content:
Underfunded, undervalued and overwhelmed - that's how social service providers describe themselves.

Charities are calling for a better partnership with government and more support as they struggle to meet rising demand from precarious funding.

Mana Communications hosted a hui in Wellington on Thursday where dozens of not-for-profit organisations gathered to discuss the challenges facing the industry.

More than 90 percent of attendees responded to a poll by Mana saying they faced funding challenges.

Several participants used the phrase "perfect storm" to describe the current difficulty of meeting rising costs while a cost-of-living crisis made providing those services more expensive.

Participants said they struggled to make lasting change with year-long government contracts.

"We need a fundraising model where we don't spend our year fundraising for next year," one attendee told the room.

As a result, charities said they often ended up competing for money from a shrinking pool of funding.

Charity funder Nikau Foundation told RNZ it had observed an increase in the number of requests for funding, and in the amounts being requested.

Value for money

On top of being frustrated with having to "beg for money", as one attendee put it, charities said they felt undervalued.

Several participants raised concerns around compliance - "the multiple, similar-but-different reporting that people have to do to keep tiny amounts of funding", one person told RNZ.

This administrative work was often not funded by grants or contracts, despite being a requirement to prove an organisation's value for money, they said.

Several charities also said they wanted funding for prevention and to not be the "ambulance at the bottom of the cliff", simply reacting to crises.

Two manuhiri, or visitors, spoke to the audience about the need for and impact of social service providers.

Denis McBride said he turned to Wellington's City Mission, where he was offered transitional housing and eventually a role in the City Mission outreach team.

He told the audience he would have gone back to jail and drugs had the mission not been there.

"I've been there for eight months now in the peer support role and I've been blessed [with] the opportunity as well as I've found my purpose, I've found my why in helping people and I heal myself every day I go to work."

Twenty-three-year-old Luta Matagi said Youth Inspire had taught her and her peers life skills and lessons they hoped to pass on to their children.

"They taught me that I can move and that my voice, my ideas and my experiences do matter in life and that we need to be heard. They make us feel listened to. They make us feel at home and also they make us feel so safe," she said, voice shaking with emotion.

Multiple charities said the stories helped remind them of the purpose of their work.

"If we started off feeling undervalued, the value of the work was demonstrated by what they said," Kathryn Ross, chief executive of counselling charity Skylight Trust, said.

Whose job is it?

Mana Communications compiled attendees' concerns and ideas into one statement, which called for a "genuine partnership between government, iwi, the sector and those who invest in our communities; we need a shared direction that extends beyond election cycles and is shaped by lived experience from the outset".

Mana Communications then moderated a panel of politicians responding to the concerns raised.

Praise for the sector was universal but there was no consensus on how the government and the sector should collaborate.

A particularly divisive question was that of responsibility for society's ills.

NZ First's Gerald Warner said his party believed the state had a responsibility to get communities thriving but that it also believed in "people helping themselves", giving a "hand-up not a handout".

"Intervention does not deprive individuals and communities of the right to exercise self-responsibility."

He argued that an overhaul of the economy would ease demand on social services.

But Tamatha Paul from the Greens said the state should guarantee human rights such as affordable healthcare and housing,

She said these differences in opinion got in the way of the cross-party collaboration necessary for long-term change, especially when it involved financial investment.

"Our system is set up to scrap with each other rather than to find those areas of consensus."

Others were more hopeful.

Labour's Helen White cited her cross-party work on rough sex and strangulation as an example of bipartisan collaboration.

She said she heard the sector's frustration and said there was a possibility for more collaboration between the sector and the state, sharing responsibility for helping communities between the local and governmental levels as appropriate.

Opportunity's Kayla Kingdon-Bebb said her party saw providers as a "genuine partner" to government rather than as a "cost to be managed".

World.title: 'Eye of the storm': Business owner's fight to keep nail tech siblings in country
World.content:
A Whangārei beauty salon owner says her business may face trouble if she cannot find a way to keep her siblings in the country.

Anna Vu owns AV Beauty Spa, and has worked in the city for 12 years.

She said she had always struggled to find suitably skilled nail technicians and beauty staff and so had recruited her three siblings to work with her, from Vietnam.

Vu said they came from a poor family and her mother died while they were young. The siblings were separated growing up because their father could not care for them all. Vu said they left school early because the family did not have enough money to pursue their education.

Their father died in 2017 and the siblings reunited in 2018 to mark the first anniversary. "One of my greatest wishes was that somehow we could be together again after spending so much of our lives apart. I also hoped that one day my family might be able to help me with the business I had built, particularly during periods when my health meant I needed to slow down or rest."

Vu suffers from lupus nephritis.

She said her older sister had become a New Zealand resident through the 2021 resident visa pathway. But her two younger siblings arrived on work visas that are set to expire in early December next year and they face a much more difficult process.

They do not meet the English requirements to apply for a residence visa.

Vu has written to her local MP, Shane Reti, asking for help. "After spending so many years separated from my siblings, having the opportunity to finally work together as a family has meant more to me than I can properly put into words," she wrote to him.

She said her business would not be able to carry on in its current form without her siblings. She had recently invested in new, larger premises with room for 10 staff. Including her siblings, she had eight.

"From a purely business perspective, losing several experienced staff members within a short period would place enormous pressure on the salon. I am therefore trying to prepare early and do everything correctly rather than waiting until it is too late."

AV Beauty Spa. Supplied / AV Beauty Spa

She had been advertising for staff but said it seemed most trained nail technicians and beauty therapists wanted to set up their own businesses, rather than work for someone else.

She said her siblings were all paying tax on their earnings, being paid good wages, and were willing to work the busy late nights, weekends and public holidays that some local staff did not want to cover.

"My concern is that I am being asked to replace people who are already trained, trusted, productive and fully integrated into our business with workers whom I simply cannot find locally."

Reti's office suggested she seek advice from an immigration adviser or immigration lawyer.

Immigration adviser Katy Armstrong, of Into NZ Immigration, said the English requirement might only be one part of the family's problem.

Immigration adviser Katy Armstrong. Supplied by Katy Armstrong

"The only person that can waive English language requirements is the minister and I think they would do that quire reluctantly."

She said, beyond that, nail technicians were a difficult industry to bring people into the country in. They are on Immigration New Zealand's new "red list" of six roles that are considered high risk. Nail technicians, beauty therapists, hair or beauty salon managers, hairdressers, hospitality, retail and service managers, massage therapists and general retail managers are not eligible for the skilled work experience pathway or the trades and technician pathway to residence.

"She sounds totally legitimate and I completely get her plight but unfortunately she's in an area of work that is associated with high-risk businesses and poor employment practices and exploitative behaviour so they've appeared on the red list.

"It doesn't mean a nail technician cannot go to residence but they need to be degree-qualified, not necessarily in beauty, they could have a degree in anything."

She said English language requirements were designed to protect people from potential exploitation. There used to be a sibling category for family reunification but that was no longer possible, she said.

"She's in the eye of the storm. Vietnam is consider high risk, beauty therapists are on the high-risk list."

She said Vu might need to apply for residency and then be prepared to appeal the decision to turn it down, but this could be an expensive process.

World.title: Emotional scenes in Whangārei as Northland touch down with Ranfurly Shield
World.content:
The return of the Ranfurly Shield to Northland, for the first time in 48 years, saw Taniwha faithful flock to Whangārei airport to welcome their team home on Friday afternoon.

Northland players were greeted with a haka from the crowd and a speech from Whangarei mayor Ken Couper as they showed off the Log o' Wood they lifted with a 36-12 victory over Canterbury on Thursday night.

More than 100 fans, including school students and some long-standing fans who have followed the team for decades, filled the airport to overflowing.

So many fans were keen to be there that the airport carpark was eventually closed with queues of cars lining the road outside the airport.

Northland’s Rivez Reihana poses for a photo with young fans and supporters. Craig Butland / Photosport

On arriving home, outside back Jade Stewart was emotional with the reception the team received.

"Must of been cutting onions everybody, never had something like that to be greeted like that is unreal."

Assistant coach Robbie Abel was also blown away with the support.

"It's been unreal today. I think going into the game we knew how important it would be for our people, our community to get a result, and to bring the Shield back.

"But to actually be able to do it, and for our boys to deliver a performance like they did, it's just been awesome."

Northland’s Rivez Reihana and team mates. Craig Butland / Photosport

Abel was not sure what other celebrations were planned but liked the idea of the Ranfurly Shield touring Te Tai Tokerau.

World.title: No guarantee shelter can be provided for every rough sleeper - officials
World.content:
Potaka responds to claims policy boosted homelessness Morning Report Download MP3 9m

Weeks before the government is set to give police powers to move on rough sleepers, officials have admitted to RNZ they can't guarantee immediate shelter for anyone on any given night.

Auckland City Missioner Helen Robinson says she's grateful it's been "formally acknowledged", but is "deeply distressed" that's the reality in the country.

It comes as the largest provider of the most immediate form of shelter tells RNZ it's managing with the resources it has, but demand is "relentless".

In June, it was reported that Ministry of Social Development (MSD) managers had performance measures related to reducing emergency housing numbers. These measures have now been refocused to achieve "sustainable housing".

At the time, the prime minister admitted he did not know there was no night shelter in Auckland for people sleeping rough.

Since then, RNZ has attempted to understand what shelter is available for someone who is sleeping rough.

Over the past month, RNZ sought clarification from both MSD and the Ministry for Cities, Environment, Regions and Transport (MCERT) - which leads the government's overall programme of work to address rough sleeping - to understand where exactly someone is supposed to go if they need shelter immediately.

After multiple requests, RNZ was finally told by MCERT "there is no guarantee that shelter can be provided for every person in every circumstance in every location".

The agency said access to accommodation was dependent on a range of factors such as "an individual's circumstances, location, service capacity, and real-time availability of accommodation and appropriate support", all of which could change quickly it said.

Robinson told RNZ she'd never had it formally acknowledged there was no guarantee, "I am distressed and I am calling for change."

Auckland City Missioner Helen Robinson. Auckland City Mission

It comes as the government's move on orders legislation, which has received strong opposition, are being progressed ahead of the election.

The law would give police the power to order people as young as 14 to move elsewhere or face a possible jail sentence if they were being disorderly, begging or rough sleeping.

It also comes following reports of rough sleepers dying outdoors overnight, a man found unresponsive in a Cuba Street doorway in Wellington and a woman found unresponsive on New Brighton beach in Christchurch. RNZ understands another rough sleeper died in Auckland in July.

So for those who had nowhere else to go, and may be told to move on, where exactly could they go?

Understanding the current situation

As recently as Sunday, the minister in charge of move on orders, Paul Goldsmith told TVNZ's Q+A there were "resources available and places available for people 24/7".

Emergency housing grants are the government's primary mechanism for providing immediate shelter to people who have "nowhere else to go" and "can't stay where they are".

Housing Minister Chris Bishop said in July emergency housing still existed "because there will always be people facing genuine housing crises".

"But now it's being used as it was always intended: as a temporary last resort."

Housing providers and social services have consistently said the governments tightened emergency housing criteria has resulted in an uptick in homelessness. That concern was raised by RNZ as early as March last year, with Community Housing Aotearoa chief executive Paul Gilberd saying again this week there was a direct link between the two.

The minister in charge of move on orders, Paul Goldsmith. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

As recently as Thursday, Serena Moran - a nurse practitioner and clinic lead at Te Aro Health Centre in Wellington - told RNZ there'd been an increase in rough sleepers she was treating, including people being released from prison with no plans to continue accessing antipsychotic medication.

She said the reality most days was treating patients who may have been assaulted and having nowhere to send them.

"I basically have to say to them, 'I'm sorry, I can't find you anywhere to stay tonight. You'll need to go back to the street. I'll give you pain relief. I'll try and make you feel as comfortable as I can'."

But ministers and MSD have consistently maintained that emergency housing remains available to anyone who meets the criteria and has a "genuine need".

Ministers and MSD have also repeatedly said that people who did not receive emergency housing could have their "needs met in another way", including through other housing pathways.

Other options include:

transitional housing;

social housing; and

immediate access transitional housing

But none of those pathways guaranteed a person sleeping rough today would have somewhere safe to sleep tonight, especially if the limited immediate access transitional housing beds were full. There were only 65 nationwide.

Kāhui Tū Kaha provided the majority of these beds and told RNZ it was managing with the resources it had, but said the demand was "relentless". It also accepted referrals from police and hospitals overnight.

On Thursday evening, it accepted an elderly woman with physical access needs and a 17-year-old who had both been sleeping on the street. It also accepted a woman becoming homeless due to family violence, and a young woman who police wanted separated from a violent partner.

Kāhui Tū Kaha said things were tight but "we're constantly juggling".

Housing minister Chris Bishop. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

What shelter is actually available tonight?

Over the past month, RNZ asked MSD and MCERT multiple times what options were available for someone sleeping on the streets to go somewhere that night - more specifically, to get a bed under a roof within 24 hours.

Through various responses and phone calls, RNZ received the following information.

RNZ was told that emergency housing "is not necessarily the best option for rough sleepers" who may have a range of complex needs and require additional support.

MSD noted there were more outreach and support services for rough sleepers announced in June by associate housing minister Tama Potaka, and referenced the additional $14.5 million attached.

"Of those who approach MSD for emergency housing, 89 percent receive either emergency housing, transitional housing, help with a private rental, or hardship assistance."

In response, RNZ asked for figures around the percentage of people who were declined emergency housing and offered "some other form of assistance", specifically actual shelter tonight - noting that someone could not sleep in a food grant, but an official information act request was required, which has since been made.

MSD also outlined that emergency housing was intended as a last resort - despite earlier stating it wasn't the "best option". Its service centre hours were between 8:30am to 5pm Monday to Friday and 9:30am to 5pm on Wednesdays.

It was possible for clients to receive a short-term grant outside of service hours, to "meet immediate housing needs until client can attend the next available appointment", but MSD wasn't able to provide the percentage of calls received outside hours and how many of those were granted without an official information act request, which has since been made.

Where possible MSD would refer people with an urgent housing need to suitable transitional housing or Housing First placements - these were funded by MCERT and generally provided more support than was available to someone in Emergency Housing.

Associate housing minister Tama Potaka. Alyse Wright

MCERT's response clarified the different housing pathways for those in need:

Housing First

This supported people experiencing "chronic homelessness" to access and remain in stable housing. Support was available for as long as needed, but you had to have been sleeping rough for at least 12 months over the past three years to be considered. Those "new" to rough sleeping weren't elegible by definition.

The government announced an additional 300 homes for Housing First in 2025, following the concerns of increased homelessness.

Transitional housing

Transitional Housing offered "short-term, temporary accommodation" for those who may be affected by a change in circumstances. It also provided tailored support. Emergency referrals could generally be accomodated here.

However, MCERT confirmed the total number of contracted transitional housing places had fallen since 2023, that's despite increasing reliance on transitional housing as an alternative to emergency housing.

It said there were around 300 less places contracted in June 2026, compared to November 2023, reflecting the "planned exit of higher-cost motel-based places, as well as routine fluctuations associated with portfolio management", MCERT said.

As well, when existing transitional housing beds were redesignated as "immediate access" beds from December 2025, MCERT did not specify those beds were replaced elsewhere in the system.

Immediate access transitional housing

This is the most immediate option available, where contracted providers could accommodate eligible households without the need to first go through "standard MSD assessment and referral processes".

MCERT confirmed:

there were only 65 immediate access transitional housing beds nationwide;

all 65 were in Auckland;

only 20 were in central Auckland

RNZ then asked one more time, "what shelter is available and can be guaranteed tonight for someone who is sleeping rough?".

World.title: Panthers NRL finals charge dealt blow by Cogger's three-match ban
World.content:
Penrith is in for a NRL finals selection dilemma after key addition Jack Cogger received a three-match ban for his high shot on Tyran Wishart.

Just when the streaky Panthers looked to have found their best option at five-eighth, Cogger received a grade-two charge that rules him out until after the first week of finals.

Unless Cogger can plead his case at the judiciary and win, the Panthers will be forced to recall out-of-favour Blaize Talagi or Perth-bound Jack Cole.

Storm's finals dream over as Penrith holds on despite triple sin-binning The Penrith Panthers hold on to beat the Melbourne Storm 22-14 and end their faint mathematical hopes of making the NRL finals.

Cogger was sent to the sin bin after rushing out of the line to hit Wishart late in the Panthers' 22-14 win on Thursday night.

He has already been suspended once this season for a similar shot, missing two weeks on that occasion for rushing out and hitting South Sydney's Ashton Ward.

If he unsuccessfully challenges his charge at the judiciary, Cogger will miss an additional game, potentially ruling him out for the remainder of the season.

Cogger also received a $3,000 fine for a shot on Storm forward Angus Hinchey earlier in the clash.

But the 29-year-old's suspension is a far bigger blow for a Penrith side fighting to lock up a top-two finish.

Cogger has been a valuable addition to the Panthers' starting side in recent weeks, proving a more assured defensive presence than Talagi.

His ball-playing has also helped take pressure off halfback Nathan Cleary, as it did during Penrith's comeback victory in the 2023 grand final.

But Cogger's illegal tackle has now opened the door for either Talagi or Cole, one of whom is set to start in the halves for next week's clash with Canterbury.

AAP

World.title: Swans captain 'deeply shocked' by scandal, denies player rift
World.content:
Sydney Swans coach Dean Cox and captain Callum Mills have denied there is a rift in their playing group as they addressed the ongoing scandal engulfing the club.

Five players — Isaac Heeney, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner, Riley Bice and James Jordon — have been stood down by the Swans for breaching the club's standards on drinking and staying out late following last Sunday's win over Essendon in Melbourne.

Police from Victoria's sexual crimes squad are investigating a report of sexual assault, which the ABC understands centres on a player allegedly touching one of the women without her consent.

Police have not made any arrests or laid charges.

Mills said he was "deeply shocked and disappointed" and said he had not witnessed anything like this behaviour before.

"We really are disappointed at the action of these five players," he said.

Dean Cox and Callum Mills addressed the media. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

"As a playing group, we fully support the club's decisions on the sanctions handed down."

Mills said the five players would have to address the playing group, but there was no rift among the players.

Cox confirmed he was not in the room at the centre of the scandal, but would not say whether other staff members or players were present, as the club denied comments suggesting more men from the Swans were present in the room.

Both men refused to answer specific questions about what happened in the hotel room, saying they were the subject of a police investigation.

The Swans players and staff observed the press conference from behind the camera. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Cox was also pressed on the club's decision to have the five suspended players driven back to Sydney from Melbourne, rather than flown.

"Decisions were made [as to] how we best support our players within the circumstances that happened," he said.

Cox admitted the club's previously acclaimed culture had "taken a hit".

"Our culture isn't perfect," he said.

"We're going to work as hard as we possibly can to get the trust back from the community, to get the culture where we desire to be, where we once had been."

Live Moment Catch up up the key moments from Dean Cox and Callum Mills's press conference from Swans HQ. The press conference is over Dean Cox and Callum Mills have finished answering questions at Swans HQ. Cox's message to Sydney's fans ahead of the weekend Cox is asked what his message is to the club's fans considering coming to this weekend's games. "I hope our fans stand by us and our club is united, our playing group is united, between both programs. "We want to show that on Sunday." Is there concern for the mental health of the players? Mills is asked whether he is concerned for the mental health of the players suspended by the club. "There's concern in every part. That's the women in the community, our players involved, the women involved. "The wellbeing of everyone involved is [of] the utmost importance." Show more

Both Cox and Mills apologised to the club's AFLW team, with Mills saying he had addressed the group personally.

"I acknowledged their pain, and I deeply apologised for the actions of a few within our group," he said.

Cox added that he hoped the supporters would still come out in force for the double-header at the SCG this weekend.

"I hope our fans stand by us and our club is united, our playing group is united, between both programs," he said.

"We want to show that on Sunday."

Sydney's men's team rounds out its home and away season with a clash against North Melbourne on Sunday afternoon at the SCG, a match preceded by an AFLW match between Sydney's women's team and Essendon's women's team at the same venue.

World.title: 'Horrific consequences': Aussie star almost hit by car in Tour of Britain
World.content:
Australian cyclist Maeve Plouffe has revealed she nearly got hit by a car while riding in this week's Tour of Britain — and has warned of potentially more "horrific consequences" for a sport already reeling from tragedy.

Plouffe, the 27-year-old former Sydney track star who grabbed Commonwealth team pursuit gold and individual silver in 2022, prompted organisers of the week-long road race to review safety procedures after she outlined her "scary" experience.

Plouffe had to withdraw from the race, having suffered a puncture during the opening stage in Cumbria on Wednesday, and her revelation on Instagram about an alarming episode with a car as she attempted to chase back to the peloton.

Plouffe posted the statement of her close call on her personal Instagram account. (Instagram/@maeveplouffe)

Her comments came only days after British rider Finlay Tarling died last week during stage eight of the Volta a Portugal after he was hit by a non-race light goods vehicle that had entered the course.

Explaining her withdrawal, Plouffe added: "While the race convoy was still in sight, and I was less than two minutes down, there were cars from the general public coming at me from all directions, including one that nearly hit me on a roundabout.

"Later on, the moto escort was wonderful, and I felt much safer.

"But considering the recent devastating events in our cycling community, it's scary to see situations like this, when we know that this can have horrific consequences, especially so soon after suffering such a tragedy."

She was referring to the death of the 19-year-old Tarling, who was killed last week in a high-speed collision with a van, which had strayed onto the road during the eighth stage of the Volta a Portugal.

British rider Finlay Tarling (right) was killed by a non-race light goods vehicle during the Volta a Portugal last week. (Getty Images: Huw Fairclough)

Before the Tour of Britain Women had begun, an emotional tribute was paid to Tarling, with his picture projected onto a large screen while all 114 riders and roadside fans joined in a minute's applause to honour him.

Tarling was the younger brother of Netcompany Ineos rider Josh Tarling, who will ride the Vuelta a España Grand Tour, which begins on Saturday, in honour of his sibling.

Organisers have swiftly taken note of Plouffe with Jonathan Day, events director of British Cycling Ventures — the commercial arm of British Cycling that organises the Tour — saying in a statement: "We're taking those comments extremely seriously."

"Rider safety is paramount and will always be treated as a priority in our planning and how we operate any race.

"We're reviewing what happened with Maeve and her team, O'Shea Red Chilli Bikes, with the seriousness and empathy these comments demand.

"We recognise this comes at an especially difficult time for the cycling community, so we want to reassure all riders, teams and fans of the sport at this time of how seriously we are treating these comments."

The race continued on Thursday with Dutch superstar Lorena Wiebes claiming her second successive stage victory between Clitheroe and Blackpool but only after that second stage had been neutralised because of a car accident.

Australian rider Georgia Baker, fresh from her golden Commonwealth Games on the track in Glasgow, was also caught up in a crash on the route.

Wiebes is 14 seconds ahead of Italy's Chiara Consonni (Canyon-SRAM zondacrypto) in the general classification as the race moves into Wales on Friday.

AAP

World.title: Alcaraz confirms US Open return amid record prize money reveal
World.content:
Carlos Alcaraz is set to return to action at the US Open, ending four months of injury torment, and will be back competing for a record grand slam winner's prize of $US5.5 million ($7.7 million) in New York.

The news of the seven-time grand slam winner's comeback at Flushing Meadows will be music to the ears of former Australian Open boss Craig Tiley, who has been able to begin his reign in charge of the US Open by announcing unprecedented riches to the players.

Seven-time grand slam champion Alcaraz has not played since April due to a concerning wrist injury.

He announced his return on Thursday in unusual fashion, with the help of football journalist Fabrizio Romano.

Romano, who is usually breaking news of big football transfers, used his catchphrase, "Here we go," to announce Alcaraz's return on Instagram, while the reigning champ repeated the message on X.

Alcaraz, who started the year by winning the Australian Open, has not played since withdrawing from the Barcelona Open in April. He has missed both the ‌French Open and ⁠Wimbledon while his great rival, Jannik Sinner, has largely dominated.

Now he is fit to return to the scene of his first grand slam triumph in 2022, when he became the youngest man to reach world number one in the rankings.

Alcaraz's return is fantastic news for Tiley, the former Tennis Australia CEO who has taken up the equivalent job at the US Tennis Association (USTA) and has been able to announce an overall prize fund of $US108 million — the first time the $US100m barrier has been broken at a slam.

Alcaraz's 2026 season has been cruelled by a wrist injury. (Getty Images: Quality Sport Images/Alvaro Medranda)

It is the biggest prize pot in the sport's history and represents a 20 per cent rise for the second consecutive year.

"This is a significant first step in a multi-year investment in athletes as the US Open continues to be the best economic opportunity for players and the most valuable platform in tennis for players, fans and partners," Tiley said.

"We are proud to deliver record-setting prize money and expanded player benefits as well as providing a new platform to work together with players."

That platform is the formation of a Grand Slam Player Council, which is intended to give players a voice on a range of issues such as prize money.

Organisers hope all this will ward off the kind of player protests that occurred at the French Open and Wimbledon.

The champions' winning cheque will be $US5.5 million, up from the $5 million that Sabalenka and Alcaraz won last year.

Players will earn $US140,000 just for making it into the main draw, while a quarterfinalist earns $US780,000, a semifinalist $US1.45 million and runners-up $US2.8 million.

Meanwhile, there was good news for the Australian challenge following the withdrawal of Spain's Alejandro Davidovich Fokina from the main draw through injury.

It meant Alexei Popyrin was able to be advanced to the main draw and the reciprocal wildcard he had been given by the USTA could instead go to his Australian teammate Dane Sweeny, who will make his Flushing Meadows debut at 25.

That takes the current Australian contingent set to start the action on August 30 to a total of 14 — eight men and six women — with more attempting to make it through next week's qualifying.

AAP

World.title: Swans' decision a step towards accountability, but misogyny at AFL core
World.content:
On Wednesday, the Sydney Swans announced that five players — Riley Bice, Nick Blakey, Isaac Heeney, James Jordon and Chad Warner — would be banned for the remainder of the AFL season, inclusive of finals, for breaching club standards.

CEO Matthew Pavlich and chairperson Andrew Pridham were clear that the sanctions related to partying late at night, drinking and bringing women back to their hotel, and did not relate to sexual assault allegations or infer guilt on any party.

Concurrently, Victoria Police's Sexual Crime Squad is investigating an alleged sexual assault that occurred at the Pullman Hotel that evening.

It is not known who the allegation is against, but previous conversations about the merits of the AFL introducing a "no fault stand down policy", such as the one employed by the NRL, have centred around the message it sends to have players take the field who are facing such matters.

The club itself defined the suspensions as a "torpedoing" of its season; in effect acknowledging that the standards breach issue was and should be bigger than sport.

Andrew Pridham (right) and Matthew Pavlich addressed the media on Wednesday. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

The NRL policy, implemented in 2019, sees players automatically stood down if they face serious jail charges (those carrying a jail sentence of 11 or more years).

To be clear, this is not the situation currently being faced by the AFL players, with no charges having been laid.

But the purpose of the NRL policy is to send the message — as then ALRC commission chairperson Peter Beattie put it — "that the game does not tolerate violence against women or children."

The AFL's lack of such a policy has previously seen players such as Jordan de Goey — who in 2021 continued to play while charged with indecent assault, a charge that was later withdrawn — take to the field.

While players are entitled to the presumption of innocence until they clear their name, it is worth asking if this sends the wrong message about the seriousness of the issue of violence and disrespect of women.

The Swans' decision, then, is one step on the road to accountability.

The five players sanctioned by the club include (clockwise from top left) James Jordon, Riley Bice, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner and Isaac Heeney. (ABC News/Getty Images)

Catharine Lumby, an academic who worked as a gender advisor to the NRL for 15 years, welcomed the move as the "least they should do".

"Whether they like it or not, these young men are role models to younger men and society in general," Professor Lumby told the ABC.

Patty Kinnersly, CEO of Our Watch, Australia's national body for the prevention of violence against women, which works closely with the AFL, echoed those sentiments.

"We know that sporting stars and clubs in this country are influential, and they literally reach millions of people, and so when we see our sporting stars behaving well, setting an example, that really feeds through the rest of the community," she told ABC's 730.

"As a sports-loving nation, what sporting organisations do actually does influence how other people behave and act."

Accountability means reckoning with misogynistic cultures

The Swans' move comes at a time for the AFL to engage in a more thorough reckoning with a misogynistic culture that enables the conditions for violence against women, or disrespect of women, to occur.

When Pridham was asked about educating the players on respect for women, for example, he replied that "our male team have by and large always displayed complete respect for women, so I don't think that's something that's of concern".

Pavlich, meanwhile, added that "all I've seen so far at this football club, barring this significant incident, is that we are one club and we treat and respect women incredibly well".

The Swans AFLW team will play a double header with the men's side for the first time this weekend. (Getty Images: Sarah Reed)

The problem is, an "incident" like an allegation of sexual assault cannot be counted out or treated as an exception to the norm.

They also do not arise out of a vacuum, but in an Australian Rules Football culture that overlooks the seriousness of such allegations, especially when it comes to "stars" of the game.

When Nicky Winmar's statue was swiftly removed after his domestic violence conviction in July, for example, many rightly pointed to the irony of the AFL continuing to have Wayne Carey, who pleaded guilty in 1996 to indecent assault, in its Hall of Fame.

This week's events provided a chance for the Swans' leadership, and the AFL more generally, to take a stand on not just a breach of club standards, but the issue of sexual assault more broadly, as one with no place in the game.

"It's just a bunch of blokes PR-ing at the moment," Professor Lumby said, adding that she wanted to hear from the team's AFLW players and senior female leaders.

"I want to see the research [proving the club's respect for women]. Make it public. What do you know about off-field culture? Also show me the money when it comes to who you're employing. What about how many women are in senior positions?"

The rest of the Swans playing group has continued training ahead of the final game of the home and away season. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

Rachael Burgin, a senior lecturer at Swinburne University, and CEO of Rape and Sexual Assault Research and Advocacy (RASARA), added that the Swans' move was not necessarily a "win for accountability".

"Sydney have really focused on how the players breached the standards of the club, but this was defined as only about being out late and drinking," Dr Burgin said.

"It's absolutely a missed opportunity to say that sexual violence — even separately to the report made by a woman on Monday morning — is also a significant breach of club standards.

"Sexual violence impacts every aspect of a victim-survivor's life. Victim-survivors bear the physical, emotional, psychological and economic costs. Yet, the fact that a woman has made a report to police of sexual violence is completely invisible.

"Club leaders can comment on the broader national conversation without discussing the investigation.

"The AFL and clubs need to take responsibility for the culture that allows rape and sexual assault to thrive in Australia."

Cultural change could start with AFL making public stand

Times like these test the passion of women who are committed fans of the men's game.

Following men's sport has always been deeply conflicted; to love the game at the same time as being routinely appalled by the off-field behaviour of the men who may represent your team on field.

The Swans trumpet themselves as being an inclusive club, including hosting an annual Pride match. (Getty: Kelly Defina)

The latest sexual assault allegations also provide an opportunity for renewed conversation about what broader action the AFL could be taking to stamp out violence against women.

Lily Fetter, member of The University of Melbourne's WEAVERs, a group of women who have experienced domestic, family violence and/or sexual violence, and co-design research projects and training programs, argues this could start with the introduction of a dedicated round.

"When it comes to tackling domestic and sexual violence, it's an enormous problem," Fetter said.

"It's an epidemic and it's not going to be fixable by one individual. It takes a whole of community response, and that's where organisations like the AFL have such a wide reach and a really significant level of influence.

"Can you imagine [how powerful it would be] in the lead-up to the grand final, if the AFL took a lead in things like public advertising to say 'family violence is not OK, you're not alone and there's support out there'?"

Many female fans have conflicted feelings about supporting the men's teams.

Dr Burgin agreed with Fetter that the "AFL is one of the most powerful cultural institutions in this country", but said holding a themed round could be seen as tokenistic if deeper cultural changes were not made.

"Holding a round to raise awareness of violence against women is performative, when the AFL is complicit in constructing Australia's misogyny problem," she said.

"We need national standards for how sporting clubs prevent and respond to violence against women, transparent reporting on clubs' compliance with those standards and we need governments to regulate that.

"Frankly, women in this country who love and play football, including those in the ALFW, deserve a competition that takes their safety as seriously as it takes the score."

World.title: Runner breaks national record with 436km over 65 hours
World.content:
Among the lines of dialogue Clint Eastwood set into cinematic immortality is one about everyone having to know their limitations.

For competitors of a recent ultramarathon race named in honour of the Hollywood actor, however, those limitations were very ambitious indeed.

In the case of Yuko Sato, they extended to 436 kilometres over the course of 65 hours straight — "course" being something of an operative word.

The runner recently completed that distance by doing laps around a public green space in suburban Brisbane.

Such was the scale of the challenge that it paid to think only a few steps ahead.

"I don't know how I did it," Sato said.

Yuko Sato at the Clint Eastwood Last One Standing at Rocklea over the weekend. (Supplied: Yuko Sato)

What started with ambition ended with something bordering on apparition.

"I was hallucinating. I saw lots of plastic models hanging over the trees, both sides," she said.

"I didn't sleep at all.

"The next day I started to swell in the foot and now I can't fit into any shoes, so probably [for the] next three-to-five days I can't run."

Sato is an ultramarathon runner and competes in a gruelling format called a "backyard ultra".
